ethics_check.report:
Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, but it was not present:

> In the PWI task, participants are asked to name pictures while ignoring a simultaneously presented distractor word (often presented as a word superimposed on the picture) or a non-lexical string (such as "XXXX").

> In the CN task, participants are presented with a sequence of non-repetitive pictures to name.

> Four groups of 5,000 participants were simulated in a picture naming task, governed by Equations 1-4 described above.

> Stimulus order and congruency conditions were randomized independently for each participant.

> Recall that the study interleaved trials from a linguistic task (PWI) and a non-linguistic visuospatial task (PP), in which participants had to ignore a large prime arrow and indicate the direction of a smaller probe arrow by pressing one of the four buttons for the four directions (up, down, left, and right arrows).

> The order of both stimulus and congruency conditions were randomized independently for each participant.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. stat_effect_size.title: Effect Sizes in t-tests and F-tests
stat_effect_size.summary_text: All detected t-tests and F-tests had an effect size reported in the same sentence.

table.text: Statistical analyses supported the cumulative semantic interference observed in human participants (β = 13.78, SE = 0.60, t = 23.13, p < .001).

When comparing across lags (i.e., 2, 4, 6, 8), we found a main effect of ordinal position (β = 12.33, SE = 1.46, t = 8.45, p < .001), no effect of lag (β = -0.99, SE = 0.89, t = -1.11, p = .27), and no interaction between the two (β = 0.29, SE = 0.27, t = 1.09, p = .28), mirroring the empirical findings.

When comparing across lags (i.e., 2, 4, 6, 8), we found a main effect of ordinal position (β = 12.33, SE = 1.46, t = 8.45, p < .001), no effect of lag (β = -0.99, SE = 0.89, t = -1.11, p = .27), and no interaction between the two (β = 0.29, SE = 0.27, t = 1.09, p = .28), mirroring the empirical findings.

live_data_statements: In the PWI task, participants are asked to name pictures while ignoring a simultaneously presented distractor word (often presented as a word superimposed on the picture) or a non-lexical string (such as "XXXX").
In the CN task, participants are presented with a sequence of non-repetitive pictures to name.
Four groups of 5,000 participants were simulated in a picture naming task, governed by Equations 1-4 described above.
Stimulus order and congruency conditions were randomized independently for each participant.

Recall that the study interleaved trials from a linguistic task (PWI) and a non-linguistic visuospatial task (PP), in which participants had to ignore a large prime arrow and indicate the direction of a smaller probe arrow by pressing one of the four buttons for the four directions (up, down, left, and right arrows).
The order of both stimulus and congruency conditions were randomized independently for each participant.

info.title: A learning account of cognitive control in word production: A path to new insights into the domain generality of control

author.affiliation:
Department of Psychological and Brain Sciences
								Indiana University

Department of General and Applied Psychology
								Ghent University

Department of Psychological and Brain Sciences
								Indiana University

text.text: Various computational models have been proposed to explain interference and its resolution in word production.
Of these, incremental learning models provide an elegant explanation of the interfering effects of the similarity between a target word and its context.
However, such models have not been extended to explain how the production system deals with other kinds of interference, such as the presence of a prepotent distractor.
It thus remains unclear whether incremental learning can furnish a general mechanism for explaining interference and its resolution in word production.
This paper proposes the Cognitive Control, Production, and Learning Model (CoCo-PaLM), a comprehensive learning-based model of interference and control in word production.

In addition to capturing the previously modeled effects, CoCo-PaLM predicts sequential effects of control, as well as effects involving the transfer of control between the language system and non-linguistic systems.

More broadly, the model establishes learning as a computational principle for explaining interference and control and offers a framework for dissociating the neural domain-generality of control from its implementation in specific domains.
Cognitive control is the regulation of cognition and behavior in accordance with goals (e.g., Braver, 2012).
text.formatted: Cognitive control is the regulation of cognition and behavior in accordance with goals (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Braver, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: In language production, control plays a prominent role, as speakers have many choices in terms of message, words, and syntactic structures to fulfill their communicative goals (Nozari, 2018; Quinn et al., 2025).
text.formatted: In language production, control plays a prominent role, as speakers have many choices in terms of message, words, and syntactic structures to fulfill their communicative goals <ref type="bibr" target="#b213">(Nozari, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b250">Quinn et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: While the relevance of cognitive control to production is undisputed, the mechanisms by which control is implemented remain vague.
The goal of this paper is to provide an account of how word production is controlled, and how such control interfaces with control in non-linguistic tasks.

We limit the scope of our investigation to single-word (as opposed to phrase or sentence) production, to have room to examine different kinds of interference involved in this seemingly simple operation.
We maintain, however, that the principles derived from this investigation can be extended to the production of larger linguistic chunks.
This study has two goals: a language-specific goal and a more general goal.
The languagespecific goal is to deliver a computational model of control in word production.
We show that a language model, without appealing to language-external structures, can capture a number of empirical findings.
At the same time, we demonstrate the shortcomings of that model in capturing other effects.

On this basis, we argue that control in word production is best implemented as a hierarchical model, in which the core language model is embedded in a "domain-general" monitoring and control loop shared between the language production system and other cognitive systems (e.g., Acheson & Hagoort, 2014; Fedorenko, 2014; Fedorenko & Thompson-Schill, 2014; Piai et al., 2013; Wessel & Anderson, 2024; Wolna et al., 2024).
text.formatted: On this basis, we argue that control in word production is best implemented as a hierarchical model, in which the core language model is embedded in a "domain-general" monitoring and control loop shared between the language production system and other cognitive systems (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Acheson & Hagoort, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b101">Fedorenko, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b103">Fedorenko & Thompson-Schill, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b242">Piai et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b335">Wessel & Anderson, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b341">Wolna et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: We demonstrate that this hierarchical model, CoCo-PaLM (Cognitive Control, Production, and Learning Model), accounts for what the existing models of interference in word production account for, as well as new findings.
text.formatted: We demonstrate that this hierarchical model, <ref type="bibr">CoCo-PaLM (Cognitive Control, Production, and Learning Model)</ref>, accounts for what the existing models of interference in word production account for, as well as new findings.

text.text: CoCo-PaLM also allows us to test the study's second goal, which is to develop an account of how domain-general neural systems implement control in specific domains.
A central issue that we must confront is the distinction between neural and functional mechanisms.

A tacit assumption in the field is that neural domain-generality (i.e., shared neural substrates of control across tasks) leads to functional domain-generality (i.e., transfer of control from one task to another; e.g., Hussey et al., 2017; Ness et al., 2023; cf. Nozari & Martin, 2024; Nozari & Novick, 2017).
text.formatted: A tacit assumption in the field is that neural domain-generality (i.e., shared neural substrates of control across tasks) leads to functional domain-generality (i.e., transfer of control from one task to another; e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b151">Hussey et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b211">Ness et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr">cf. Nozari & Martin, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b226">Nozari & Novick, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: The assumption of functional domain-generality, in turn, underlies practices such as brain training, where training using a simple computerized task is expected to generate broad benefits for everyday functions (e.g., Au et al., 2015; Jaeggi et al., 2008; Klingberg, 2010; Schweizer et al., 2011), even though the empirical support for such benefits is in question (Gobet & Sala, 2023; Melby-Lervåg & Hulme, 2013; Owen et al., 2010; Redick et al., 2013; Sala et al., 2019; Sala & Gobet, 2019; Simons et al., 2016).
text.formatted: The assumption of functional domain-generality, in turn, underlies practices such as brain training, where training using a simple computerized task is expected to generate broad benefits for everyday functions (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Au et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b155">Jaeggi et al., 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b161">Klingberg, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b284">Schweizer et al., 2011)</ref>, even though the empirical support for such benefits is in question <ref type="bibr" target="#b126">(Gobet & Sala, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b199">Melby-Lervåg & Hulme, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Owen et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b255">Redick et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Sala et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Sala & Gobet, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b296">Simons et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: We explore this assumption computationally by augmenting the core language model with a domain general control loop and simulating known empirical effects of the transfer of control between language and non-language tasks.
The link between the two goals is not arbitrary.

To understand the implementation of cognitive control in lexical retrieval, which is the primary goal of this research, one must determine whether control in language production is domain-general or not.
At the same time, language production is an excellent and often neglected tool for studying cognitive control.
It is a naturally complex and highly generative task, which is nevertheless well-practiced.

These characteristics allow us to go beyond artificial forced-choice button-press tasks with very limited response sets and arbitrary stimulus-response mappings often used in studies of cognitive control.

Thus, our framework is highly informative for understanding the implementation of control, more generally, by providing a mechanistic account of the relationship between neural domain-generality and functional domain-specificity within and across control-demanding tasks.
We focus on tasks that require response selection; we do not address response inhibition in the form of withholding a response (Verbruggen & Logan, 2008; Wessel & Aron, 2017).
text.formatted: We focus on tasks that require response selection; we do not address response inhibition in the form of withholding a response <ref type="bibr" target="#b319">(Verbruggen & Logan, 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b336">Wessel & Aron, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Throughout the paper, we use the term "interference" to refer to the behavioral manifestation of task difficulty, such as slow responses or errors.
The mechanism underlying interference in our tasks is "conflict" or simultaneous co-activation of multiple responses that compete for selection (e.g., Botvinick et al., 2001).
text.formatted: The mechanism underlying interference in our tasks is "conflict" or simultaneous co-activation of multiple responses that compete for selection (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Botvinick et al., 2001)</ref>.

text.text: We use the term "monitoring" to refer to a continuous process of collecting information about the ongoing state of the system.

In our model, this is achieved by continuously surveying conflict levels among units representing potential responses (Botvinick et al., 2001; Nozari et al., 2011; Verguts & Notebaert, 2008; Yeung et al., 2004).
text.formatted: In our model, this is achieved by continuously surveying conflict levels among units representing potential responses <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Botvinick et al., 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b218">Nozari et al., 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Verguts & Notebaert, 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b348">Yeung et al., 2004)</ref>.

text.text: Finally, we use the term "control" to refer to the active adjustments in the system, in response to the information collected by the monitor, at the service of optimizing performance in accordance with task goals (Braver, 2012; Nozari, 2025b).
text.formatted: Finally, we use the term "control" to refer to the active adjustments in the system, in response to the information collected by the monitor, at the service of optimizing performance in accordance with task goals <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Braver, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b217">Nozari, 2025b)</ref>.

text.text: The current study targets lexical retrieval, a key component of word production.
We chose lexical retrieval, as it is one of the most well-studied phenomena in language production (Dell, 1986; Goldrick et al., 2014; Levelt, 1989; Levelt et al., 1999).
text.formatted: We chose lexical retrieval, as it is one of the most well-studied phenomena in language production <ref type="bibr" target="#b82">(Dell, 1986;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Goldrick et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b175">Levelt, 1989;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b176">Levelt et al., 1999)</ref>.

text.text: To produce a word, speakers must first activate the concept behind the word.
This concept may be activated by external stimuli (e.g., a picture of a cat, real objects like the cat itself, etc.), or internally, via memory recall.
It is now largely accepted that concepts are represented in a distributed network, with potential hubs to connect and condense individual features (Lambon Ralph et al., 2017).
text.formatted: It is now largely accepted that concepts are represented in a distributed network, with potential hubs to connect and condense individual features <ref type="bibr" target="#b173">(Lambon Ralph et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: The concept activates abstract lexical representations, which carry grammatical information such as grammatical gender for nouns or argument structures for verbs, but do not represent forms (Caramazza, 1997; Dell, 1986; Garrett, 1980).
text.formatted: The concept activates abstract lexical representations, which carry grammatical information such as grammatical gender for nouns or argument structures for verbs, but do not represent forms <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">(Caramazza, 1997;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b82">Dell, 1986;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b120">Garrett, 1980)</ref>.

text.text: In the next stage, lexical items are mapped onto their segments (phonemes in spoken and graphemes in written production); those segments are sequenced, and finally commands are sent to motor effectors for execution.
This study focuses on the first stage of this process, namely, the mapping of semantic features onto lexical items.
The challenge here is that such mapping is not exclusive to the target.
Other lexical items that share some of the semantic features with the target item are simultaneously activated.
For example, upon seeing the picture of a cat, other furry four-legged animals, such as dogs, also come to mind, and their lexical entries are correspondingly activated.
This co-activation creates conflict during selection (e.g., Nozari et al., 2011).
text.formatted: This co-activation creates conflict during selection (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b218">Nozari et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Evidence for such conflict comes from a large body of work showing that introducing semantically related items (e.g., "dog" for the target "cat"), either as distractor words or as previously named items, causes interference in naming the target (Belke et al., 2005; Damian & Martin, 1999; Howard et al., 2006; Ganushchak & Schiller, 2008; Glaser & Düngelhoff, 1984; Lupker, 1979; see Bürki et al., 2020, for a meta-analysis).

text.text: While this interference is relatively mild and often manifests in slowed response times in neurotypical individuals, it often leads to overt semantic errors in individuals with post-stroke damage to the language system (aphasia; Dell et al., 1997; Schwartz et al., 2009), showcasing the necessity for the successful resolution of conflict during lexical selection.

text.text: Resolving conflict in lexical selection has often been tied to domain-general cognitive control, mostly through correlational analysis: researchers have examined the correlation between the size of interference in a generic cognitive control task, such as Stroop (Stroop, 1935), flanker (Eriksen & Eriksen, 1974), Simon (Simon, 1969; Simon & Rudell, 1967; Simon & Wolf, 1963), etc., or a combination of control tasks (e.g., Miyake et al., 2000) and performance on some aspect of lexical retrieval.

text.text: If the analysis of individual differences is difficult to interpret as a means of investigating the involvement of control in lexical retrieval, what is the alternative?
Here, we lay out a blueprint of such an approach in four steps and carry out those steps in the following sections.
As explained earlier, interference is simply a behavioral observation; it does not define a mechanism.
It is usually mediated by underlying conflict, which relies on monitoring and control for its resolution.
At this stage, the key question is: Is all conflict resolved using the same mechanism or not?
Answering
A very large body of literature has examined interference in word production, using different kinds of paradigms.

These studies can generally be divided into two groups: those that have investigated the interference induced by the similarity between a target and its context (contextual similarity), and those that have examined the interference induced by the presence of a strong non-target alternative that biases processing away from the target (prepotent response).

These two sources of interference have clear relevance to everyday language production and may even coexist: many conversations involve mentioning items from the same category (e.g., what ingredients to buy for cooking dinner, which clothing items to match for a party, etc.).
Moreover, many social conversations demand overriding a prepotent response.
For example, if a dish you are served at a dinner party naturally evokes the word "terrible", you may have to override that response with the word "delicious" when asked for your opinion.
The paradigms used for examining these two effects are also some of the most well-known and widely used paradigms in psycholinguistic research.
Below, we provide a brief summary of these paradigms and their main findings.

Contextual similarity refers to the interference that arises when a target item shares semantic or segmental features with other items in the context in which it is produced (Belke et al., 2005; Breining et al., 2016; Harrison et al., 2020; Nozari, Freund, et al., 2016; Schnur et al., 2006 Schnur et al., , 2009)).
text.formatted: Contextual similarity refers to the interference that arises when a target item shares semantic or segmental features with other items in the context in which it is produced <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Belke et al., 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Breining et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b135">Harrison et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b219">Nozari, Freund, et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b279">Schnur et al., 2006</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b280">Schnur et al., , 2009))</ref>.

text.text: Most relevant to lexical selection, which is the primary focus of this paper, is semantic similarity.
Semantic similarity itself can be divided into taxonomic and thematic similarity (Mirman et al., 2017; Zhai et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Semantic similarity itself can be divided into taxonomic and thematic similarity <ref type="bibr" target="#b206">(Mirman et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b349">Zhai et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b351">Zhang et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Taxonomic similarity refers to items within the same category (e.g., cat, dog, sheep; category of animals).
Thematic similarity refers to items that do not belong to the same categorical cohort, but often co-occur around a theme (e.g., balloon, cake, present; theme of a birthday party).

Generally speaking, taxonomic, but not thematic, relations cause interference in language production (Alario et al., 2000; Belke & Stielow, 2013; Costa et al., 2005; Damian & Martin, 1999; Howard et al., 2006; Mahon et al., 2007; Oppenheim & Nozari, 2024; see Nozari & Pinet, 2020, for a review).
text.formatted: Generally speaking, taxonomic, but not thematic, relations cause interference in language production <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Alario et al., 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Belke & Stielow, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">Costa et al., 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b72">Damian & Martin, 1999;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b145">Howard et al., 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b186">Mahon et al., 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b232">Oppenheim & Nozari, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr">see Nozari & Pinet, 2020</ref>, for a review).

text.text: Since our focus is on interference and its resolution, we focus on studies of taxonomic similarity, hereafter simply referred to as contextual similarity.

Two paradigms have often been used to study pure contextual similarity in picture naming (i.e., without additional demands, such as the suppression of prepotent responses): continuous naming (CN) and blocked-cyclic naming (BCN) paradigms.
In the CN paradigm, participants name a series of pictures containing exemplars from the same semantic category.

Reaction times (RTs) increase linearly as a function of the ordinal position of the item within the target category, demonstrating a clear cumulative interference effect (e.g., Alario & Moscoso del Prado Martín, 2010; Howard et al., 2006; Schnur, 2014).
text.formatted: Reaction times (RTs) increase linearly as a function of the ordinal position of the item within the target category, demonstrating a clear cumulative interference effect (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Alario & Moscoso del Prado Martín, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b145">Howard et al., 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b278">Schnur, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: In the BCN paradigm, participants name small sets of pictures that repeat across multiple cycles.

In the homogeneous condition, all items within a block are drawn from the same semantic category (e.g., dog, cat, lion, sheep, cow), whereas in the heterogeneous condition, items are drawn from different semantic categories (e.g., dog, shirt, boat, pear, book).

Although mean RTs generally decrease across cycles in both conditions, RTs in the homogeneous blocks are consistently longer than those in the heterogeneous blocks starting from cycle 2, demonstrating clear semantic interference (e.g., Belke et al., 2005; Damian et al., 2001; Schnur et al., 2006; Shao et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Although mean RTs generally decrease across cycles in both conditions, RTs in the homogeneous blocks are consistently longer than those in the heterogeneous blocks starting from cycle 2, demonstrating clear semantic interference (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Belke et al., 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">Damian et al., 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b279">Schnur et al., 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b287">Shao et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: However, whether this interference continues to accumulate across cycles or stabilizes after the first cycle remains debated in the literature; some studies report cumulative interference across cycles (e.g., Schnur et al., 2006), while others fail to observe such accumulation (e.g., Belke, 2013; see Wöhner & Jescheniak, 2026, for a review).
text.formatted: However, whether this interference continues to accumulate across cycles or stabilizes after the first cycle remains debated in the literature; some studies report cumulative interference across cycles (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b279">Schnur et al., 2006)</ref>, while others fail to observe such accumulation (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Belke, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr">see Wöhner & Jescheniak, 2026</ref>, for a review).

text.text: In short, both CN and BCN paradigms reveal a robust contextual interference as a function of taxonomic similarity between the target and context.
Although both tasks tap contextual similarity, it is important to note that each has a unique place in the language literature.

Specifically, CN addresses lexical retrieval without repetition, whereas BCN focuses on the repeated production of a small group of items, a situation that is often used in training vocabulary in a new language or re-training vocabulary after brain damage (e.g., Nozari et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Specifically, CN addresses lexical retrieval without repetition, whereas BCN focuses on the repeated production of a small group of items, a situation that is often used in training vocabulary in a new language or re-training vocabulary after brain damage (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b220">Nozari et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: This difference brings in additional complexities to BCN, including priming effects and a possible role for working memory (Belke & Stielow, 2013; in later cycles, naming each picture makes the remaining pictures more predictable), possibly explaining the differences observed in the cumulativeness of interference (Crowther & Martin, 2014).
text.formatted: This difference brings in additional complexities to BCN, including priming effects and a possible role for working memory <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Belke & Stielow, 2013</ref>; in later cycles, naming each picture makes the remaining pictures more predictable), possibly explaining the differences observed in the cumulativeness of interference <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">(Crowther & Martin, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Interference can also arise from the need to suppress a prepotent non-target response, which is commonly investigated with the picture-word interference (PWI) paradigm (Lupker, 1979; Rosinski et al., 1975).
text.formatted: Interference can also arise from the need to suppress a prepotent non-target response, which is commonly investigated with the picture-word interference (PWI) paradigm <ref type="bibr" target="#b181">(Lupker, 1979;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b266">Rosinski et al., 1975)</ref>.

text.text: In the PWI task, participants are asked to name pictures while ignoring a simultaneously presented distractor word (often presented as a word superimposed on the picture) or a non-lexical string (such as "XXXX").

Previous research has shown that RTs and error rates are significantly higher when the distractor is a word compared to a non-lexical string, indicating that the interference is driven by the lexical properties of the distractor rather than its visual features (e.g., Piai et al., 2016).
text.formatted: Previous research has shown that RTs and error rates are significantly higher when the distractor is a word compared to a non-lexical string, indicating that the interference is driven by the lexical properties of the distractor rather than its visual features (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b241">Piai et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Furthermore, when the distractor word is the actual name of the picture (the congruent condition), performance is better than when it does not (incongruent condition; e.g., Glaser & Düngelhoff, 1984; La Heij, 1988).
text.formatted: Furthermore, when the distractor word is the actual name of the picture (the congruent condition), performance is better than when it does not (incongruent condition; e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b124">Glaser & Düngelhoff, 1984;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b169">La Heij, 1988)</ref>.

text.text: It is worth mentioning that PWI has also been used to demonstrate interference arising from contextual similarity by manipulating the relationship between the picture and the superimposed distractor.
The general finding matches that discussed in the previous section: taxonomic relationships interfere with production.

For example, the incongruent trial with the target picture of a "cat" and the taxonomically related distractor word "dog" creates more behavioral interference than the incongruent trial with the picture of a "cat" and the unrelated distractor word "pen" (Costa et al., 1999; La Heij et al., 1990; Rayner & Springer, 1986; Schriefers et al., 1990; van der Burght & Meyer, 2025).
text.formatted: For example, the incongruent trial with the target picture of a "cat" and the taxonomically related distractor word "dog" creates more behavioral interference than the incongruent trial with the picture of a "cat" and the unrelated distractor word "pen" <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">(Costa et al., 1999;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b170">La Heij et al., 1990;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b253">Rayner & Springer, 1986;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b281">Schriefers et al., 1990;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b316">van der Burght & Meyer, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: In short, the main PWI effect is the interference created by any lexical distractor (related or unrelated) presented over a target picture.
Taxonomic relatedness of the distractor to the target can increase the overall interference effect, but this increase is small compared to the interference generated by any distractor.
When we use PWI as a prime example of a task imposing a prepotent distractor, we are focused on the main effect of lexical interference, which encompasses both related and unrelated distractors.

Although both contextual similarity and a prepotent distractor produce behavioral interference that can be successfully resolved, behavioral and neural evidence suggests distinct underlying mechanisms. Nozari, Freund, et al. (2016) presented participants with several blocks of pictures to name.
text.formatted: Although both contextual similarity and a prepotent distractor produce behavioral interference that can be successfully resolved, behavioral and neural evidence suggests distinct underlying mechanisms. <ref type="bibr" target="#b219">Nozari, Freund, et al. (2016)</ref> presented participants with several blocks of pictures to name.

text.text: Each block had only two pictures, each repeated multiple times at random.

Two manipulations were embedded in this design: (a) contextual similarity, which was manipulated by changing the relationship between the two pictures within a block (e.g., semantically related: hat/wig, initial-segment-overlap: pen/pot; final-segment-overlap: cup/map).
(b) Presence of a prepotent response was manipulated by asking participants to reverse the names of the two pictures in the second half of each block.
For example, if they saw a picture of "hat", they would have to say "wig" and vice versa.
As expected, both manipulations created behavioral interference.
However, the interference due to semantic similarity and prepotent response suppression during name reversal did not interact.

In an EEG study, Pinet and Nozari (2023) replicated the findings of Nozari, Freund, et al. (2016) with a new set of materials: they found interference, both as a function of semantic similarity and name reversal, which were orthogonal to one another.
text.formatted: In an EEG study, <ref type="bibr" target="#b244">Pinet and Nozari (2023)</ref> replicated the findings of <ref type="bibr" target="#b219">Nozari, Freund, et al. (2016)</ref> with a new set of materials: they found interference, both as a function of semantic similarity and name reversal, which were orthogonal to one another.

text.text: Classic stimulus-locked EEG analyses revealed stark differences between the electrophysiological signatures of semantic similarity and name reversal.
The two effects had opposite polarities, different timelines, and different topographies.
Response-locked analyses revealed similar effects.

Finally, a representational similarity analysis (RSA) showed a sustained effect of similarity throughout the trial, with greater similarity scores for the semantically related compared to the unrelated condition.

In contrast, a clearly biphasic electrophysiological signature was observed for name reversal, with a higher similarity score for the reversed compared to the straight trials in the first half of the trial, followed by a clear reversal of similarity scores in the second half of the trial.
This switch was interpreted as the point of control implementation to tease apart the two representations.
More recently, Pirnia et al. (2026) reanalyzed Pinet and Nozari's (2023) data with machine learning methods.
text.formatted: More recently, <ref type="bibr" target="#b246">Pirnia et al. (2026)</ref> reanalyzed <ref type="bibr" target="#b244">Pinet and Nozari's (2023)</ref> data with machine learning methods.

text.text: This is the most powerful approach to analyzing the EEG data, as it takes into account data from all 128 electrodes, for the entire trial duration, across all participants.

The authors reasoned that if there was a common mechanism for resolving conflict due to contextual similarity and name reversal, it should be possible to uncover shared high-vs. low-conflict neural states between the two trial types.

Specifically, a classifier trained to differentiate between highand low-conflict trials as defined by contextual similarity of the two words (similar vs. not similar, respectively) should be able to successfully classify high-and low-conflict trials as defined by name reversal (reversed vs. not reversed) and vice versa.
The authors showed that several classifiers, when trained on the contextual similarity data, could successfully tease apart high-vs. low-conflict trials in that task.
The same success was obtained when classifiers were trained and tested on the name reversal data.

Moreover, the study showed generalization to new participants: using a leave-one-out approach, the authors demonstrated that, when trained on the name reversal of 27 participants, the classifier could successfully classify high-vs. low-conflict states of the leftout 28 th participant in name reversal.
Finally, conflict states could be cross-classified between semantic and phonological similarity within the contextual similarity manipulation.

Despite these successful generalizations, cross-task classification between contextual similarity and name reversal was completely at chance, providing no support for common conflict states across the two sources of conflict.

To summarize, behavioral data, classic EEG analysis, RSA analysis, and classification approaches to analyzing EEG data have provided converging evidence for a separation of the mechanisms underlying conflict resolution induced by contextual similarity and a prepotent response.

This separation has a solid theoretical motivation (Nozari, 2025a): For contextual similarity, even though non-target items create competition with the target item, the stimulusdriven information leads processing towards the target as the response.
text.formatted: This separation has a solid theoretical motivation <ref type="bibr">(Nozari, 2025a)</ref>: For contextual similarity, even though non-target items create competition with the target item, the stimulusdriven information leads processing towards the target as the response.

text.text: For example, in CN, the stimulus is the picture.
In neurotypical individuals, a picture activates, first and foremost, its own label, not the label of any of the semantically similar distractors.

In contrast, in tasks such as PWI or name reversal, the stimulus information actually biases competition in favor of the non-target item to be selected as the response: the word printed on the picture (or at times spoken over the picture) has privileged access to a name response, through the reading or the auditory processing route (Mahon et al., 2007), when compared to the picture which must first be semantically decoded.
text.formatted: In contrast, in tasks such as PWI or name reversal, the stimulus information actually biases competition in favor of the non-target item to be selected as the response: the word printed on the picture (or at times spoken over the picture) has privileged access to a name response, through the reading or the auditory processing route <ref type="bibr" target="#b186">(Mahon et al., 2007)</ref>, when compared to the picture which must first be semantically decoded.

text.text: In name reversal, the presented picture strongly evokes its own name, which must be suppressed before the alternate word can be produced.
This suppression must be guided by a task goal that is set and maintained throughout the task.

Maintaining task goals is one of the most widely agreed-upon functions of domain-general control regions such as the prefrontal cortex (Braver, 2012; Duncan, 2010; Miller & Cohen, 2001; Wiecki & Frank, 2013).
text.formatted: Maintaining task goals is one of the most widely agreed-upon functions of domain-general control regions such as the prefrontal cortex <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Braver, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b94">Duncan, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b204">Miller & Cohen, 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b339">Wiecki & Frank, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: The empirical evidence reviewed above pointed to different mechanisms underlying the interference caused by contextual similarity and a prepotent response.
This section investigates their key characteristics, which, in turn, point to some similarities.
A key characteristic of interference caused by contextual similarity is that it is long-lasting and largely immune to the insertion of irrelevant items between the semantically related items.

For example, Howard et al. (2006) showed that the magnitude of semantic interference remained unaffected by lag, defined as the number of unrelated intervening items (i.e., 2, 4, 6, or 8 intervening items). Schnur (2014) also reported robust interference when 2-8 lags separated two semantically related items in CN.
text.formatted: For example, <ref type="bibr" target="#b145">Howard et al. (2006)</ref> showed that the magnitude of semantic interference remained unaffected by lag, defined as the number of unrelated intervening items (i.e., 2, 4, 6, or 8 intervening items). <ref type="bibr" target="#b278">Schnur (2014)</ref> also reported robust interference when 2-8 lags separated two semantically related items in CN.

text.text: The author further showed that under some circumstances, interference can persist across even longer lags (e.g., 14).

In a similar vein, Hepner and Nozari (2020) showed that lexical perseverations on pictures that were semantically related to a previously named item showed long lags, with median lags between 35-40 items in three individuals with aphasia who demonstrated many such perseverations.

text.text: Just like CN, BCN interference also persists despite longer intervals and insertion of unrelated items. Hsiao et al. (2009) analyzed perseverative errors (repetition of past responses for new targets) in the BCN paradigm and demonstrated that such errors can occur despite multiple intervening items within a cycle.
text.formatted: Just like CN, BCN interference also persists despite longer intervals and insertion of unrelated items. <ref type="bibr" target="#b146">Hsiao et al. (2009)</ref> analyzed perseverative errors (repetition of past responses for new targets) in the BCN paradigm and demonstrated that such errors can occur despite multiple intervening items within a cycle.

text.text: The evidence above shows that contextual similarity creates long-standing effects.
Is the same true for prepotent responses?
One of the best ways to investigate this is to examine sequential effects in PWI.
As noted above, both CN and BCN interference effects are inherently sequential effects; interference only arises because later items are associated with earlier items.
In contrast, the primary interference effect in PWI is often not sequential.
In many cases, pictures and distractor words are presented simultaneously.
However, it is possible to examine performance across different trials of a PWI task.
For example, one could examine performance on each trial as a function of the previous trial type.

Given that each trial can be either congruent (distractor word matching the picture's name) or incongruent (distractor word not matching the picture's name) four trial types arise: cC, cI, iC, and iI, where c and i denote the congruency of the previous trial, and C and I the congruency of the current trial.
A common finding when analyzing the data this way is that (iI -iC) creates smaller interference than (cI -cC).
In other words, the difference between incongruent and congruent trials shrinks after an incongruent, compared to a congruent, trial.

This is called a congruency sequence effect (CSE; Egner, 2007; Gratton et al., 1992) and is observed across a wide range of tasks with congruent and incongruent trials, including visuospatial tasks (e.g., Simon: Stürmer et al., 2002; flanker: Ullsperger et al., 2005; and prime-probe: Kunde & Wühr, 2006), and tasks that involve linguistic representations (e.g., Stroop, and PWI; Kerns et al., 2004; Freund et al., 2016).
text.formatted: This is called a congruency sequence effect (CSE; <ref type="bibr" target="#b96">Egner, 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b128">Gratton et al., 1992)</ref> and is observed across a wide range of tasks with congruent and incongruent trials, including visuospatial tasks (e.g., <ref type="bibr">Simon: Stürmer et al., 2002;</ref> <ref type="bibr">flanker: Ullsperger et al., 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr">and prime-probe: Kunde & Wühr, 2006)</ref>, and tasks that involve linguistic representations (e.g., <ref type="bibr">Stroop, and PWI;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b158">Kerns et al., 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b112">Freund et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Importantly, CSE is a long-lasting effect, resilient to the passage of time and insertion of irrelevant tasks. Freund and Nozari (2018) tested this in a task-switching paradigm by alternating PWI trials with trials from a visuospatial task called the prime-probe (PP) task (Weissman et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Importantly, CSE is a long-lasting effect, resilient to the passage of time and insertion of irrelevant tasks. <ref type="bibr" target="#b113">Freund and Nozari (2018)</ref> tested this in a task-switching paradigm by alternating PWI trials with trials from a visuospatial task called the prime-probe (PP) task <ref type="bibr" target="#b332">(Weissman et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: In the latter, a large prime arrow appeared on each trial, followed by a smaller probe arrow.
Participants indicated the direction of the probe arrow by pressing one of four buttons (up, down, left, or right).
On congruent trials, prime and probe arrows pointed in the same direction.
On incongruent trials, they pointed in different directions.
The design was perfectly balanced for examining both 2-back within-task CSE and 1-back cross-task CSE.
Results showed a robust 2back within-task CSE for both PWI and PP tasks, showcasing the longevity of the CSE.
Interestingly, no support was found for a 1-back cross-task CSE, whether from PWI to PP or vice versa, pointing to a task/domain-specific CSE (Freund & Nozari, 2018; Experiment 1).

text.text: These results were replicated in a second experiment, where PP trials were swapped for a sentence reading task.

Sentences either contained lexical or syntactic ambiguity, which is known to induce conflict (Duffy et al., 1988; Ferreira & Henderson, 1990; Grodner et al., 2002; Nelson et al., 1980), or they did not.

text.text: In summary, both contextual similarity and suppression of a prepotent response influence the following trials.
This influence is long-lasting, persisting across time and intervening unrelated trials.

The nature of the influence is distinct, though: contextual similarity creates accumulating interference over the following trials, whereas suppression of a prepotent response creates facilitation over the next incongruent trial.
Moreover, sequential effects appear to be task-specific.
Long-lasting influences that are largely immune to the passage of time and insertion of unrelated items have the distinct signature of learning.
By learning, we refer to mechanisms that go beyond the activation of neurons and instead target the connections between neural populations.

In artificial neural networks, learning is represented by the change in the strength (weights) of the connections between the nodes in the network, rather than the activation value of individual nodes, which is often subject to quick decay, making learning a more lasting mechanism than activation.

Importantly, incremental learning has been used successfully to model interference resulting from contextual similarity (e.g., Howard et al., 2006; Oppenheim, 2018; Oppenheim & Nozari, 2024; Oppenheim et al., 2010), showing the promise of this approach, at least for modeling one kind of interference.
text.formatted: Importantly, incremental learning has been used successfully to model interference resulting from contextual similarity (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b145">Howard et al., 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b230">Oppenheim, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b232">Oppenheim & Nozari, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b231">Oppenheim et al., 2010)</ref>, showing the promise of this approach, at least for modeling one kind of interference.

text.text: However, the same learning models have not been applied to tasks such as PWI, where suppression of a prepotent distractor is required.
In contrast, there are alternative accounts of interference that do not have learning mechanisms (e.g., Abdel Rahman & Melinger, 2009; Roelofs, 2018).

text.text: In the next sections, we present a detailed review of the learning and non-learning models of interference in language production, and show that, to date, no model captures all the empirical effects with a clear, simple, neurobiologically plausible mechanism.
The idea of incremental learning as the mechanism underlying semantic interference was first implemented by Howard et al. (2006) to explain semantic interference in CN.
text.formatted: The idea of incremental learning as the mechanism underlying semantic interference was first implemented by <ref type="bibr" target="#b145">Howard et al. (2006)</ref> to explain semantic interference in CN.

text.text: Their simple network consists of a semantic layer (S-units, or semantic nodesfoot_0 ) and a lexical layer (L-units, or lexical nodes).

text.text: The model has three key mechanisms: (1) shared activation, (2) competition, and (3) priming.
Upon the presentation of a stimulus, the semantic node of the target gains the most activation, with the semantic nodes of the related items also gaining partial activation (shared activation).
Activation then spreads to lexical nodes, which compete for selection via lateral inhibitory connections (competition).
Once the activation of a lexical node reaches the threshold, it is selected as the response, and the processing time until selection is recorded as the simulated RT.
After the response is selected, the connection weight between the active semantic feature nodes and the selected lexical node is strengthened by a constant proportion (priming).
Notably, this strengthening is restricted to the connection to the selected node, while connections to coactivated competitors are left unchanged.
In subsequent trials, when a member of the same semantic category is presented, interference is induced from shared activation partially activating the previously named competitor's semantic node.

Since the competitor's semantic-lexical connection has been previously strengthened, its lexical node becomes more active and thus creates stronger lateral inhibition to suppress the activation of the current target's lexical node, resulting in a longer time before the target can accumulate enough activation to reach the selection threshold.

As more items from the same category are named, the number of primed competitors accumulates, leading to an approximately linear increase in RTs across ordinal positions. Howard et al.'s (2006) model is plausible in its assumptions and elegant in its implementation, naturally generating RT distributions as a function of competition.
text.formatted: As more items from the same category are named, the number of primed competitors accumulates, leading to an approximately linear increase in RTs across ordinal positions. <ref type="bibr">Howard et al.'s (2006)</ref> model is plausible in its assumptions and elegant in its implementation, naturally generating RT distributions as a function of competition.

text.text: However, adding a constant proportion only to the selected connection is not a common learning rule in artificial networks.
The next generation of learning models offered an improvement by using a common learning function.

Oppenheim and colleagues proposed a series of incremental learning models employing the error-based delta rule (Rumelhart et al., 1986; Widrow & Hoff, 1960): The first of these was the Dark Side model (Oppenheim et al., 2010).

text.text: Similar to Howard et al. (2006), the model has two layers, mapping distributed semantic features to lexical nodes.
text.formatted: Similar to <ref type="bibr" target="#b145">Howard et al. (2006)</ref>, the model has two layers, mapping distributed semantic features to lexical nodes.

text.text: The model is a feedforward network in which semantic feature nodes (e.g., MAMMALIAN, AQUATIC) form the input layer and lexical nodes (e.g., "dog", "boat") form the output layer.
Each lexical node is connected to a set of semantic feature nodes, with semantically related words sharing some of the semantic feature nodes (e.g., "dog" and "whale" share the feature MAMMALIAN).

Every semantic feature node has potential connections directly to every lexical node, with no lateral connections within either layer, and no feedback connections from the lexical to the semantic layer.
When a stimulus is presented, activation spreads from semantic features to the lexical layer, activating the target along with competitors.
Then, a booster repeatedly and multiplicatively amplifies the activation of every lexical node until one node's activation exceeds the mean activation of all other nodes by a threshold.
At this point, the highest activated lexical node is selected as the response, and RTs are computed as a function of the number of boosting cycles required.
If no lexical node satisfies the selection rule before a fixed deadline, the trial ends in an omission error.

Importantly, after each trial, the semantic-to-lexical connections are updated based on the discrepancy between the node's actual and desired activation according to the delta rule; connections from active features to the target are strengthened, while connections from the shared features to competing non-target words are weakened.

Thus, a subsequent target in the same category requires more boosting cycles to adequately separate its activation from those recently strengthened competitors, resulting in progressively longer RTs in CN.

The same mechanism also explains the data from BCN; the model simultaneously captures repetition priming (i.e., an overall decrease in RTs in both homogeneous and heterogeneous conditions across cycles), as well as the overall advantage of the heterogeneous over the homogeneous condition. Oppenheim (2018) further extended the model to interference resulting from newly acquired words.

text.text: In short, learning models have successfully modeled long-lasting effects of contextual similarity, as well as the diverging effects of taxonomic and thematic contextual similarity.
However, they have room for improvement; some do not have a natural mechanism for simulating RTs, while others do not have a widely accepted learning function.

Most importantly, none of them has been applied to PWI, or similar tasks that require the suppression of a prepotent response, leaving a clear gap in our understanding of the extent to which incremental learning can explain interference and its resolution in language production.
The most important non-learning model of lexical interference is WEAVER and its subsequent versions (Levelt et al., 1999; Roelofs, 1992 Roelofs, , 1997 Roelofs, , 2003 Roelofs, , 2018)).

text.text: The model can also be construed as the most complete model of lexical interference to date, as it has been applied to CN, BCN, and PWI, although it has not attempted to capture CSE.

The model consists of three layersa conceptual layer with lexical concept nodes, a syntactic layer with lemma nodes, and a wordform layer containing morphological, phonological, and phonetic representations.
The conceptual layer consists of non-decompositional semantics, meaning each lexical concept is represented by a single, independent node rather than a distributed set of semantic features.
To capture semantic similarity, the conceptual layer organizes nodes into a semantic network connected by explicit, labeled links (e.g., IS-A link; Collins & Loftus, 1975; Quillian, 1969).

text.text: When a stimulus is presented, its corresponding conceptual node is activated and sends a proportion of its activation through the semantic network to other connected concept nodes.
The activation simultaneously spreads through the network, activating nodes in the lemma layer.
Lemma selection follows a competitive selection rule based on Luce's choice ratio (Luce, 1959).
text.formatted: Lemma selection follows a competitive selection rule based on Luce's choice ratio <ref type="bibr" target="#b180">(Luce, 1959)</ref>.

text.text: At each timepoint, the selection probability of a lemma is determined by the ratio of its own activation to the summed activation of all co-activated lemmas (Roelofs, 1992).

text.text: In its original form, the model does not account for interference either in contextual similarity or suppression of a prepotent response; therefore, different extensions have been used to account for different kinds of interference.
To account for the interference effects observed in the PWI paradigm, Roelofs (2003) added an executive verification process.
text.formatted: To account for the interference effects observed in the PWI paradigm, <ref type="bibr" target="#b264">Roelofs (2003)</ref> added an executive verification process.

text.text: Rather than blindly selecting the most active lemma, an executive production rule checks the explicit goal of the task.
In the PWI task where the goal is to name a picture, this control rule blocks the input from the irrelevant written word.

However, this blocking mechanism operates with a slight temporal latency, allowing the distractor word to gain a temporary head start in activation, driving up the early-stage competition and thereby slowing the RT for the target picture name.
As explained earlier, the idea of goal-setting is critical for explaining the overriding of a prepotent response, since stimulus-driven information simply will not get one to the correct response.
However, it is unclear why the implementation of goals should work with a delay built into the model, when the task goal is known to the speaker from the start.
To capture the semantic interference observed in CN and in BCN, Roelofs (2018) proposed a new extension.
text.formatted: To capture the semantic interference observed in CN and in BCN, <ref type="bibr" target="#b265">Roelofs (2018)</ref> proposed a new extension.

text.text: Specifically, after a lexical concept node is selected in each naming trial, a constant bias term is added to that specific concept node's activation in subsequent same-category item trials.
This constant activation term is added iteratively and exclusively to items from the same semantic category in both CN and BCN.
For example, in BCN, the first cycle has no bias.
A bias of 2.5 units is introduced in the second cycle, and an additional bias of 2.5 is manually added in each subsequent cycle (e.g., 5, 7.5, 10, and so on).
This incremental addition of a bias increases the lexical competition for the current target.
As a result, the target word requires more time steps to accumulate enough activation to win competitive selection, hence the increase in RTs.
Roelofs (2018) motivated this manipulation by appealing to the fact that conversations usually form around a theme, giving rise to a temporary conceptual bias for that theme.

Conceptual priming is a reasonable assumption, but by the same assumption, it can be argued that conceptual biases are short-lived; when the topic of conversation shifts, interlocutors can flexibly and quickly shift their attention to new topics.

Given that we are specifically interested in long-lasting effects that survive irrelevant items (in CN) and blocks (in BCN), it is reasonable to ask why conceptual bias towards a given semantic category after a gap not only never decays but is continuously amplified despite the presence of irrelevant items and other categories in between.
In that sense, it may be better construed as a form of learning.

Another important non-learning framework for explaining interference is Abdel Rahman and Melinger's (2009) Swinging Lexical Network, aimed specifically at explaining semantic interference and facilitation effects within PWI and BCN.
The framework inherits its two-level architecture of conceptual and lexical layers from WEAVER, where conceptual nodes can be connected via shared category or associative relationship.

The framework also retains competitive lexical selection with two additional assumptions: (1) lexical competition is only strong enough to produce interference when an interrelated cohort of competitors, rather than a single isolated competitor, is co-activated; and (2) the semantic context simultaneously triggers conceptual facilitation via priming of the target concept, and lexical competition via lexical cohort activation.

The polarity of the net behavioral effect is thus determined by the trade-off between conceptual facilitation and lexical competition, which ultimately hinges on the size of the co-activated lexical cohort.

The most important contribution of the Swinging Lexical Network has been its explanation for the dual effect of semantic similarity observed in PWI, namely interference with a categorical distractor (e.g., Glaser & Düngelhoff, 1984; Glaser & Glaser, 1989; La Heij, 1988; Lupker, 1979; Lupker & Katz, 1981 , 1982; Schriefers et al., 1990) and facilitation with an associative distractor (e.g., Alario et al., 2000; Bölte et al., 2013; La Heij et al., 1990; Lupker, 1979).
text.formatted: The most important contribution of the Swinging Lexical Network has been its explanation for the dual effect of semantic similarity observed in PWI, namely interference with a categorical distractor (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b124">Glaser & Düngelhoff, 1984;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b125">Glaser & Glaser, 1989;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b169">La Heij, 1988;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b181">Lupker, 1979;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b182">Lupker & Katz, 1981</ref> <ref type="bibr">, 1982;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b281">Schriefers et al., 1990)</ref> and facilitation with an associative distractor (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Alario et al., 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Bölte et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b170">La Heij et al., 1990;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b181">Lupker, 1979)</ref>.

text.text: When the distractor is categorically related to the target, both items share a superordinate category node, causing the activation to converge on and co-activate a whole cohort of related lexical competitors.
This highly interconnected cohort creates strong one-to-many lexical competition that overwhelms conceptual priming, resulting in delayed RTs, or interference.
In contrast, when the distractor is associatively related but belongs to a different category, activation spreads to mutually unrelated nodes in different categories and does not converge.
This produces only one-to-one competition, which is insufficient to overrule the conceptual priming benefit, yielding a net decrease in RTs, or facilitation.
The same mechanism is also extended to explain interference in the BCN paradigm.
In a homogeneous block, repeatedly naming items from the same category activates a shared category node, which spreads activation to an interrelated lexical cohort.
The resulting one-tomany competition overcomes conceptual facilitation and causes interference in RTs.
Conversely, in a heterogeneous block, unrelated items do not produce convergent activation, thus no competition or interference arises.
The Swinging Lexical Network does not have a computational implementation, which makes it difficult to fully understand its mechanisms and predictions.
Also, the longevity of interference induced by contextual similarity may not be easy to explain with the Swinging Lexical Network.
As such, the only implementation of a non-learning account of interference and control in language production remains to be Roelofs (2018).
text.formatted: As such, the only implementation of a non-learning account of interference and control in language production remains to be <ref type="bibr" target="#b265">Roelofs (2018)</ref>.

text.text: This model has the unique advantage of capturing performance across CN, BCN, and PWI, which no other model does.
However, some of the model's assumptions, such as non-decaying conceptual priming and delayed goal implementation, are questionable or may be variants of learning.
Finally, even this model does not explain sequential effects in control implementation in the form of CSEs.
The previous section demonstrated that much insight has been gained from the various models of interference in language production.

At the same time, it highlighted some important shortcomings, ranging from implementational issues (e.g., unnatural methods of RT simulation, etc.) to scope (i.e., lack of a single model that captures all the empirical data).
The goal of this study is to propose a model that addresses these shortcomings.

text.text: This choice is motivated by two facts: (a) as reviewed in earlier sections, both types of interference show long-lasting effects that can be most elegantly captured by learning models, and (b) there is now growing evidence that incremental learning underlies many aspects of language production, such as repetition priming (e.g., Howard et al., 2006), phonotactic learning (e.g., Dell et al., 2000; Warker, 2013; Warker & Dell, 2015; Warker et al., 2008 Warker et al., , 2009) ) and orthotactic learning (e.g., Atilgan & Nozari, 2026; Pacton et al., 2001; see Dell et al., 2021, for a review).

text.text: Given this state of literature, and the success of several computational models in modeling interference induced by contextual similarity with learning (Howard et al., 2006; Oppenheim, 2018; Oppenheim et al., 2010; Oppenheim & Nozari, 2024), we aim to test the explanatory power of incremental learning as the common principle underlying conflict generation and its resolution.

text.text: We further propose that the differences observed between the two types of interference simply arise from incremental learning, implemented as synaptic changes between representational elements, in different parts of the system.

Specifically, incremental learning within the core language system accounts for findings related to contextual similarity, whereas learning between the core system and the domain-general control regions accounts for findings related to the presence of a prepotent distractor.

The general architecture of CoCo-PaLM (Figure 1) consists of a domain-specific module embedded in a domain-general monitoring-control loop (Botvinick et al., 2001 (Botvinick et al., , 2004;; Kerns et al., 2004; Nozari, 2018; Nozari et al., 2011).

text.text: The domain-specific module in this model can be any cognitive module (e.g., visual processing).
Since the current study focuses on language production tasks, the core model is a model of lexical retrieval.
This core model implements stimulus-driven processing (i.e., the stimulus-response, or the S-R mapping 2 ).
The monitoring-control loop implements top-down processing (i.e., goal setting and maintenance).
This loop also receives information from the response layer of the core model to assess task difficulty and enhances input processing accordingly to optimize task performance.

One of the main claims of this study is that the core model is sufficient when S-R mapping generally steers processing towards the correct response, as in the case of contextual similarity (CN and BCN).
Conversely, the larger monitoringcontrol loop is necessary when simple S-R mapping leads processing away from the target response, as in the case of prepotent distractors (PWI).
The model is a neural network, working with the basic principles of spreading activation and incremental learning (Dell, 1986; Hebb, 1949; McClelland et al., 1986).

After each trial, the model undergoes changes to optimize its performance on future trials, based on the current information.

text.text: In the CN task, participants are presented with a sequence of non-repetitive pictures to name.
Items from a target category are separated by a specific number of intervening unrelated items.
The number of intervening items is referred to as lag (Howard et al., 2006).
text.formatted: The number of intervening items is referred to as lag <ref type="bibr" target="#b145">(Howard et al., 2006</ref>).

text.text: An item's ordinal position indicates its presentation order within the category.
For example, in the sequence dog, car, chair, cat, with the target category being "animals", dog is at ordinal position 1, and cat is at ordinal position 2, with a lag of two.
Four groups of 5,000 participants were simulated in a picture naming task, governed by Equations 1-4 described above.
Each simulated participant named five target pictures from the same semantic category.
The groups differed in lag (2, 4, 6, and 8) as in empirical experiments (Howard et al., 2006; Schnur, 2014), leading to different total number of trials.

text.text: Importantly, analyses focused on the target pictures in ordinal position 1-5.
RTs generated in these positions were averaged and analyzed using a linear mixed-effects regression model with the lme4 package in R v4.4.1 (Bates et al., 2014).

In a second model, we examined the interference as a function of lags.
This model included ordinal position, lag, and the interaction between the two as fixed effects, as well as intercepts for participants.
To evaluate the robustness of the model, we conducted a parameter space search for the combinations of selection threshold (k) and the Hebbian learning rate (η).
The selection threshold ranged from 3.5 to 5.5 (step size = 0.25) and the learning rate from 0.005 to 0.015 (step size = 0.001).
Each coordinate in the resulting parameter space represents the outcomes from 1,000 simulated participants.
The resulting heatmap shows the t-statistics for the slope of RTs across ordinal positions, thresholded for statistical significance using a two-sided test with 𝛼𝛼 = .05.

text.text: Since weight adjustments are determined by the concurrent activation of semantic features and word nodes, processing an unrelated intervening item strengthens only the connections for that specific word.
Furthermore, since the intervening item shares no semantic features with the target category, these localized updates do not affect the connection weights in the target category.
As a result, the number of intervening trials (i.e., lag condition) does not influence the RT of naming the subsequent target-category item.

In summary, results of Simulation 1 showed that the dynamics of the core model closely captured the data pattern observed in CN, showed robustness in a large part of the parameter space, and correctly reproduced the additional finding of RT invariance across lags.
In Simulation 2, we simulated BCN with the exact same parameters as in Simulation 1.
Recall that in BCN, participants repeatedly name a small set of pictures across multiple cycles.
In the homogeneous condition, all items within the set belong to the same category, whereas in the heterogeneous condition, the items are drawn from distinct categories.

Two key observations are as follows: (1) average RTs in heterogeneous blocks are faster than in homogeneous blocks from cycle 2 onward; and (2) average RTs decrease overall as cycles progress, reflecting repetition priming (e.g., Schnur et al., 2006; Figure 5a).

text.text: We simulated 5,000 participants, each completing one homogeneous block and one heterogeneous block.
Each block consisted of four cycles of five trials, yielding 20 trials per block.
The generated RTs were analyzed using the same analytical approach used in Simulation 1.
The model included condition (i.e., homogeneous vs. heterogeneous), cycle (i.e., 1-4), and their interaction as fixed effects, as well as random intercepts for participants.
To evaluate the robustness of the model, we conducted a parameter space search for the combinations of selection threshold (k) and the Hebbian learning rate (η).
The selection threshold ranged from 3.5 to 5.5 (step size = 0.25) and the learning rate from 0.005 to 0.015 (step size = 0.001).
Each coordinate in the resulting parameter space represents the outcomes from 1,000 simulated participants.

The resulting heatmap shows the t-statistics for the semantic interference in RTs (i.e., mean RTs in homogeneous condition -mean RTs in heterogeneous condition), thresholded for statistical significance using a two-sided test with 𝛼𝛼 = .05.

text.text: In summary, the results of Simulation 2 demonstrated that the same learning model used to capture the results of the CN task also successfully captured the pattern of results in the BCN task.
Recall that in PWI, participants name a picture that either matches a distractor word superimposed on it (congruent) or not (incongruent).
Unlike in CN and BCN, simple S-R mapping often leads to selecting the prepotent distractor rather than the target.

However, humans can perform the task with high accuracy by setting and maintaining goals (Duthoo et al., 2014; Freund et al., 2016; Schriefers et al., 1990; Shitova et al., 2017; van Maanen & van Rijn, 2010).

text.text: Simulation 3 tests whether the core model, which does not have a goal-setting mechanisms, can capture the basics of human performance in this task.

To simulate the PWI paradigm, we expanded the core model to include a stimulus letter layer for the written distractor, with three letter nodes connected to the corresponding word node in the response layer, simulating a simple word-reading route.
Prepotency of the distractor was modeled as stronger letter-to-lexical connection weights (l).
Specifically, the same input of 0.1 was given to the three letter nodes connected to word with weights of 0.002, leading to an input of 0.0006 to the distractor.

As such, the distractor was, on average, 1.2 times as much input as the target, making it the prepotent response in line with previous computational implementations of Stroop-like tasks with a prepotent response (e.g., Verguts & Notebaert, 2008).

text.text: Activation, selection, and weight updating were carried out using Equations 1-4.
We simulated 5,000 participants, each completing 64 congruent and 64 incongruent trials.
In congruent trials, identical pictures and words were simulated.
In incongruent trials, each target picture was paired with a distractor word from the same semantic category.
Stimulus order and congruency conditions were randomized independently for each participant.

As expected, this model had an unreasonably high error rate in incongruent trials of 65.56% ± 0.15%, indicating that without top-down control from the task goal, the model commonly selected the highly activated prepotent distractor.

As demonstrated with the previous set of simulations, although the core lexical retrieval model successfully resolves conflict arising from contextual similarity, it cannot overcome a prepotent distractor on its own.
This section introduces CoCo-PaLM, which situates the core model into a domain-general monitoring-control loop.

This extension allows us to (a) complete our model of interference in language production, and (b) test the second goal of the paper, which is investigating whether neural domain-generality of control necessarily leads to the transfer of control across tasks.
Importantly, we maintain incremental learning as the core mechanism responsible for generating and resolving interference in this model.
Figure 6 shows the hierarchical architecture of CoCo-PaLM, comprising the core language model, embedded in a domain-general monitoring-control loop.
text.formatted: Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_8">6</ref> shows the hierarchical architecture of CoCo-PaLM, comprising the core language model, embedded in a domain-general monitoring-control loop.

text.text: A second, non-language, task has also been embedded under this loop to model the transfer of control between the language and non-language tasks.
The core language model is simply the model used in Simulations 1-3.
The monitoring and control loop is adapted from the adaptation-by-binding model (Verguts & Notebaert, 2008 , 2009).
text.formatted: The monitoring and control loop is adapted from the adaptation-by-binding model <ref type="bibr">(Verguts & Notebaert, 2008</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">, 2009)</ref>.

text.text: This is a model of Stroop-like tasks, with a stimulus layer, a response layer, a monitoring center that tracks conflict, and a control center that represents the task goals via task nodes (Rainer et al., 1998).
text.formatted: This is a model of Stroop-like tasks, with a stimulus layer, a response layer, a monitoring center that tracks conflict, and a control center that represents the task goals via task nodes <ref type="bibr" target="#b251">(Rainer et al., 1998)</ref>.

text.text: On each trial, the model encounters a congruent or an incongruent trial, and response conflict is compared to the average conflict experienced in the task.
This difference is then used by the control center to adjust the connection weights between the task nodes in the control center and the stimulus layer through a learning function.
The key element in the adaptation-by-binding model is the implementation of control through learning.

It is not simply the activation of the task nodes that matters in biasing competition away from the irrelevant and towards the relevant information, but the strength of the connections between those nodes and task-specific representations.

If one practices task A, a certain set of connections between the control center and the representations involved in task A will be trained, leading to improved performance in task A. However, the connections between the control center and task B remain untrained.

This instantiation of control as learning allows the model to successfully capture within-task CSE in the absence of cross-task CSE, supported by the empirical data (Akçay & Hazeltine, 2011; Egner et al., 2007; Freund & Nozari, 2018; Funes et al., 2010; Kiesel et al., 2006; Kim & Cho, 2014; Notebaert & Verguts, 2008; Wendt et al., 2006 Wendt et al., , 2014;; Zhang et al., 2025; Zhu, Wang, et al., 2025).

text.text: We adopted a similar architecture for CoCo-PaLM.
Domain-specific processes, such as default stimulus-response mapping, are carried out within the modules and are subject to withinmodule incremental learning.
At the same time, goal-driven behavior is implemented as learning that takes place between the domain-specific module and the domain-general control center.
The PWI model is implemented as in Simulation 3.
A monitoring center is added that continuously computes the conflict between the two most highly activated responses and relays this to the control center.
To give neural domain-generality of control its best shot, we only implemented a single pair of relevant (R) and irrelevant (IR) task nodes in the control center (c) (cf., Verguts & Notebaert, 2008).
