text.text: Task nodes are connected to relevant and irrelevant dimension nodes in the dimension (d) layer, with the same initial weights 𝑤𝑤 𝑐𝑐𝑐𝑐 (Verguts & Notebaert, 2008).
text.formatted: Task nodes are connected to relevant and irrelevant dimension nodes in the dimension (d) layer, with the same initial weights 𝑤𝑤 𝑐𝑐𝑐𝑐 <ref type="bibr">(Verguts & Notebaert, 2008)</ref>.

text.text: For PWI, the relevant dimension (picture) projects to all semantic feature nodes and the irrelevant (word) dimension to all letter nodes with the same weights (𝑤𝑤 𝑐𝑐𝑖𝑖 ).
The dimension layer is often absent in computational models of tasks such as Stroop, where control is usually implemented by changing the weights between task nodes and stimulus nodes.
Such direct implementation works well for tasks with limited S-R mappings and many repetitions, as all items will be quickly trained within a few iterations of the task.
However, repetition is not necessary for producing CSE.
PWI tasks often have a large set of unique items that are not frequently repeated, and yet the task produces robust CSE (Freund et al., 2016; Freund & Nozari, 2018; Zhu, Wang, et al., 2025).
text.formatted: PWI tasks often have a large set of unique items that are not frequently repeated, and yet the task produces robust CSE <ref type="bibr" target="#b112">(Freund et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b113">Freund & Nozari, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b354">Zhu, Wang, et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: The quick generalization to new items indicates that the trained mapping is not between individual items, but rather, constitutes training a broader strategy of biasing processing towards the relevant information and away from the irrelevant information.
We represent such information in a dimension layer.
Dimensions are task-dependent; in PWI, the relevant dimension is the picture, and the irrelevant dimension is the written word.
In a Stroop task, the relevant dimension is the color, and the irrelevant dimension is the word.

The addition of the dimension layer allows us to modulate control effects by adjusting the weights between task nodes and dimensions, rather than the stimulus layer directly (see Cohen et al., 1990, for a related approach to control implementation).

If a task contains mostly congruent trials, indeed the best strategy might be to use all input information, whereas a task with a high proportion of incongruent trials will benefit from stronger inhibition of the irrelevant information.
The model naturally captures this flexibility.
Simulation 5.
Interleaved PWI and PP:
The Interaction Between a Language and a Non-language Task Simulation 4 revealed that CoCo-PaLM could successfully capture CSE in PWI.
However, two sets of empirical findings remain to be tested with the model.
First is the longevity of CSE and its persistence against the passage of time and intervening tasks.
Second is the absence of crosstask CSE.
To test these two effects, we simulated the data from Freund and Nozari (2018).
text.formatted: To test these two effects, we simulated the data from <ref type="bibr" target="#b113">Freund and Nozari (2018)</ref>.

text.text: Recall that the study interleaved trials from a linguistic task (PWI) and a non-linguistic visuospatial task (PP), in which participants had to ignore a large prime arrow and indicate the direction of a smaller probe arrow by pressing one of the four buttons for the four directions (up, down, left, and right arrows).

Long-lasting within-task CSE was assessed by analyzing the interaction between the current congruency and 2-back congruency, whereas cross-task CSE was analyzed as the interaction between the current and 1-back congruency.
The structure of the PWI task and its parameters were identical to Simulation 4.
We simply add a PP task to the model (Figure 6; Table 2).
text.formatted: We simply add a PP task to the model (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_8">6</ref>; Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_1">2</ref>).

text.text: The stimulus of the PP layer consisted of eight nodes: four representing the large prime arrow directions and four representing the small probe arrow directions.
These stimulus nodes projected to the response layer, which consisted of four nodes representing the response options.

As in the adaptation-by-binding model (Verguts & Notebaert, 2008), the prime arrows had stronger connections to the response nodes than probe arrows, ensuring the prime arrow direction is the prepotent response.
text.formatted: As in the adaptation-by-binding model <ref type="bibr">(Verguts & Notebaert, 2008)</ref>, the prime arrows had stronger connections to the response nodes than probe arrows, ensuring the prime arrow direction is the prepotent response.

text.text: The connection weights from the probe arrow to the response nodes were set to 0.005, consistent with the total semantic features weight for a word in the PWI task.
The prime-to-response connection weights were set at 1.2 times of the probe-to-response weights at 0.006, consistent with the input ratio applied in the PWI task.
To represent task goals, the same relevant task node in the control center was connected to the "small" dimension, which is how the target probe arrows are represented in the task.
The irrelevant task node was, in turn, connected to the "large" dimension (Figure 6).
text.formatted: The irrelevant task node was, in turn, connected to the "large" dimension (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_8">6</ref>).

text.text: The steps and functions used for simulating PP were identical to those used for PWI.
Given the different neighborhood, input and threshold were adjusted to match accuracy/mean RT to human data (Table 2).
text.formatted: Given the different neighborhood, input and threshold were adjusted to match accuracy/mean RT to human data (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_1">2</ref>).

text.text: We simulated 5,000 participants, each completing 128 trials of PWI and 128 trials of PP, with half of trials in each task being congruent and the other half incongruent.
The two tasks strictly followed an ABAB task-switching paradigm with all sequences starting with PWI, aligning with the design of Freund and Nozari (2018).
text.formatted: The two tasks strictly followed an ABAB task-switching paradigm with all sequences starting with PWI, aligning with the design of <ref type="bibr" target="#b113">Freund and Nozari (2018)</ref>.

text.text: The order of both stimulus and congruency conditions were randomized independently for each participant.
The analytical approach was similar to Simulation 4, except that previous congruency was determined by a 2-back trial for within-task CSE and a 1-back trial for cross-task CSE.
Four sets of analyses were conducted: within-task CSE for PWI, within-task CSE for PP, cross-task CSE from PWI to PP, and cross-task CSE from PP to PWI.
The analytical method aligned with the empirical study (Freund & Nozari, 2018), evaluated using linear mixed-effects models with the lme4 package in R v4.4.1 (Bates et al., 2014).

text.text: For both the RT and error-rate analyses, the model included fixed effects for current congruency, previous congruency, and their two-way interaction to assess the CSE.
Significance for the models were evaluated using Satterthwaite approximations (Kuznetsova et al., 2017).

text.text: To summarize the results of Simulations 4 and 5, implementing control as learning the connection weights between the domain-general control center and task-specific representations allows CoCo-PaLM to correctly capture within-task CSE in both PWI and PP, in the absence of a positive cross-task CSE.

text.text: Simulations were run in Python 3.11 and statistical analyses of simulated data were conducted in R v4.4.1.
No new empirical data were collected; empirical data used for comparison were taken from published studies, as cited in each simulation.
This study was not preregistered.

This project had two goals: (a) to build a model of interference and control in lexical retrieval that could account for CN, BCN, PWI, and sequential effects of adaptive control, and (b) to use that model to examine the transfer of control between language and non-linguistic tasks and test the functional domain-generality of control.
CoCo-PaLM achieved both goals.
We showed that learning mechanisms could account for data patterns in all three tasks and provide a natural explanation for the longevity of sequential effects.

We also showed that since learning resides in the connection between representations, and not representations themselves, even fully domaingeneral control representations will still lead to largely domain-specific control implementation.

CoCo-PaLM builds on previous language models, but it is novel in several respects: First, while previous models of interference in language production have captured contextual similarity effects with learning mechanisms within the core language system (e.g., Howard et al., 2006; Oppenheim, 2018; Oppenheim et al., 2010; Oppenheim & Nozari, 2024), CoCo-PaLM extends learning to the connection between the language system and a domain-general monitoring-control loop.
text.formatted: CoCo-PaLM builds on previous language models, but it is novel in several respects: First, while previous models of interference in language production have captured contextual similarity effects with learning mechanisms within the core language system (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b145">Howard et al., 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b230">Oppenheim, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b231">Oppenheim et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b232">Oppenheim & Nozari, 2024)</ref>, CoCo-PaLM extends learning to the connection between the language system and a domain-general monitoring-control loop.

text.text: Second, CoCo-PaLM naturally accounts for both RTs and error rates, while using wellmotivated learning rules.
The third advantage of CoCo-PaLM over previous models is its robust and interpretable parameters.
We have intentionally kept the model parameters to a minimum, explained them conceptually, and have kept them constant across simulations, when theoretically motivated.
For example, the parameters used for simulating CN (Simulation 1) were kept unchanged for the simulation of BCN (Simulation 2).
Similarly, the domain-general parameters were kept constant across the simulation of language and non-linguistic tasks, despite different neighborhoods (Simulations 4 and 5).

Moreover, all the core language models' parameters were kept the same when the model was embedded in the domain-general monitoring-control loop, to faithfully capture the hierarchical nature of CoCo-PaLM.
Finally, the hierarchical architecture of CoCo-PaLM allows for studying the interaction between control in language and non-linguistic tasks.
Simulation 5 showed such an interaction between two tasks, but the architecture can easily be extended to include more tasks with different neighborhoods.
Importantly, CoCo-PaLM provides a framework for studying how dimensional overlap may modify cross-task transfer of control (Zhu, Kaiser, et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Importantly, CoCo-PaLM provides a framework for studying how dimensional overlap may modify cross-task transfer of control <ref type="bibr" target="#b353">(Zhu, Kaiser, et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: We have so far shown that when the dimensions that determine relevance to task goals differ between two tasks, the model does not exhibit a positive CSE, in line with a large body of empirical data (Akçay & Hazeltine, 2011; Egner et al., 2007; Freund & Nozari, 2018; Funes et al., 2010; Kiesel et al., 2006; Notebaert & Verguts, 2008; Wendt et al., 2006; Zhang et al., 2025; Zhu, Wang, et al., 2025; see Braem et al., 2014, for a review).

text.text: In the rest of the General Discussion, we unpack some of the key modeling choices and results in terms of their theoretical and practical implications.

Traditional computational models typically treat connection weight changes as analogous to long-term synaptic strengthening or weakening (Grossberg, 2013; McClelland et al., 1995; O'Reilly & Munakata, 2000; Rumelhart & McClelland, 1986).
text.formatted: Traditional computational models typically treat connection weight changes as analogous to long-term synaptic strengthening or weakening <ref type="bibr" target="#b131">(Grossberg, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b193">McClelland et al., 1995;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b235">O'Reilly & Munakata, 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Rumelhart & McClelland, 1986)</ref>.

text.text: This treatment is also common in models of language production.

For example, smaller connection weights are used to represent an immature production system in children (e.g., Budd et al., 2011 Budd et al., , 2012;; Hanley et al., 2016) or a damaged production system in adults (e.g., Dell et al., 1997; Nozari et al., 2010; see Dell et al., 2014, for a review).
text.formatted: For example, smaller connection weights are used to represent an immature production system in children (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Budd et al., 2011</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Budd et al., , 2012;;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b133">Hanley et al., 2016)</ref> or a damaged production system in adults (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b83">Dell et al., 1997;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b223">Nozari et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr">see Dell et al., 2014</ref>, for a review).

text.text: While this view is certainly apt for representing long-term structural changes to the system, it is not the only kind of learning at play.

For example, people can quickly learn new task rules and implement them with only a handful of practice trials (Cole, Laurent, & Stocco, 2013; MacLeod & Dunbar, 1988; Palenciano et al., 2019; Ranti et al., 2015; Ruge & Wolfensteller, 2010).
text.formatted: For example, people can quickly learn new task rules and implement them with only a handful of practice trials <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">(Cole, Laurent, & Stocco, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b185">MacLeod & Dunbar, 1988;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b238">Palenciano et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b252">Ranti et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b268">Ruge & Wolfensteller, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, they can quickly switch those rules, if need be (Braver, 2012; Monsell, 2003).
text.formatted: Moreover, they can quickly switch those rules, if need be <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Braver, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b208">Monsell, 2003)</ref>.

text.text: This ability is impaired in patients with prefrontal damage, suggesting that this kind of rapid rule learning and implementation is likely to be related to the function of domain-general control regions (Aron et al., 2004; Duncan, 2010; Luria et al., 1964; Milner, 1963; see Badre & Nee, 2018, for a review).
text.formatted: This ability is impaired in patients with prefrontal damage, suggesting that this kind of rapid rule learning and implementation is likely to be related to the function of domain-general control regions <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Aron et al., 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b94">Duncan, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b184">Luria et al., 1964;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b205">Milner, 1963;</ref> <ref type="bibr">see Badre & Nee, 2018,</ref> for a review).

text.text: However, long-term structural changes are not the only form of change in the communication between neurons.
One alternative is the communication-through-coherence (CTC) framework (Fries, 2005 (Fries, , 2015)).
text.formatted: One alternative is the communication-through-coherence (CTC) framework <ref type="bibr" target="#b114">(Fries, 2005</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b115">(Fries, , 2015))</ref>.

text.text: CTC posits that effective neural communication relies less on fixed anatomical connections, but more on the relative phase alignment of rhythmically fluctuating excitability windows across sending and receiving neural populations.

Empirical evidence demonstrates that this phase-dependent routing is hierarchically organized via cross-frequency coupling-the overarching control rhythm (e.g., theta band) orchestrates the phase alignment of content-carrying rhythms (e.g., gamma band) associated with competing stimuli (Akam & Kullmann, 2012; Bosman et al., 2012; Deco & Kringelbach, 2016; Fiebelkorn & Kastner, 2019; Spyropoulos et al., 2018; Tiesinga & Sejnowski, 2010; Voloh et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Empirical evidence demonstrates that this phase-dependent routing is hierarchically organized via cross-frequency coupling-the overarching control rhythm (e.g., theta band) orchestrates the phase alignment of content-carrying rhythms (e.g., gamma band) associated with competing stimuli <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Akam & Kullmann, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Bosman et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b81">Deco & Kringelbach, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b105">Fiebelkorn & Kastner, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b299">Spyropoulos et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b314">Tiesinga & Sejnowski, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b325">Voloh et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Within the domain of language production, the theta-band oscillatory dynamics are often investigated through the PWI paradigm.
MEG evidence demonstrates a theta-power (4-8 Hz) increase in incongruent compared to congruent trials (Piai et al., 2014).
text.formatted: MEG evidence demonstrates a theta-power (4-8 Hz) increase in incongruent compared to congruent trials <ref type="bibr" target="#b243">(Piai et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: More generally, this mid-frontal theta signature has been taken as the signature of top-down control recruitment to resolve the competition between the picture and distractor processing streams (Cui et al., 2024; Krott et al., 2019; Shitova et al., 2017;  but see Zheng & Piai, 2025, for a different oscillatory profile in older adults).
text.formatted: More generally, this mid-frontal theta signature has been taken as the signature of top-down control recruitment to resolve the competition between the picture and distractor processing streams <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">(Cui et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b166">Krott et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b291">Shitova et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr"/> but see <ref type="bibr" target="#b352">Zheng & Piai, 2025</ref>, for a different oscillatory profile in older adults).

text.text: Accordingly, in our model, the rapid weight adjustments between the control center and the task-relevant and irrelevant dimensions can be taken to represent the theta-driven rhythmic gating, which orchestrates large-scale networks through phase resetting to route processing towards task-relevant goals (Verbeke & Verguts, 2019; Verguts, 2017).
text.formatted: Accordingly, in our model, the rapid weight adjustments between the control center and the task-relevant and irrelevant dimensions can be taken to represent the theta-driven rhythmic gating, which orchestrates large-scale networks through phase resetting to route processing towards task-relevant goals <ref type="bibr" target="#b318">(Verbeke & Verguts, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b320">Verguts, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Increasing the connection weight is analogous to the control center aligning its theta rhythm with the task-relevant sensory network (Cavanagh & Frank, 2014; Cohen, 2014).
text.formatted: Increasing the connection weight is analogous to the control center aligning its theta rhythm with the task-relevant sensory network <ref type="bibr">(Cavanagh & Frank, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">Cohen, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: The resulting phase reset ensures that incoming task-relevant signals arrive during the high-excitability phase of the oscillatory cycle, facilitating cross-frequency coupling and amplifying the corresponding functional impact without requiring structural synaptic changes (Canolty & Knight, 2010; Fiebelkorn & Kastner, 2019; Helfrich & Knight, 2016; Lakatos et al., 2008; Lisman & Jensen, 2013; Riddle et al., 2021; Voloh & Womelsdorf, 2016; Womelsdorf et al., 2007).
text.formatted: The resulting phase reset ensures that incoming task-relevant signals arrive during the high-excitability phase of the oscillatory cycle, facilitating cross-frequency coupling and amplifying the corresponding functional impact without requiring structural synaptic changes <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">(Canolty & Knight, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b105">Fiebelkorn & Kastner, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b141">Helfrich & Knight, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b171">Lakatos et al., 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b179">Lisman & Jensen, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b257">Riddle et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b326">Voloh & Womelsdorf, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b342">Womelsdorf et al., 2007)</ref>.

text.text: In contrast, decreasing the connection weight maps onto the control-driven phase misalignment.

By intentionally keeping competing rhythms out of phase, the control center ensures that task-irrelevant distractors arrive during the low-excitability trough of the cycle, effectively attenuating the interfering signals (Bonnefond & Jensen, 2012; Helfrich et al., 2018; Huang et al., 2015; Mathewson et al., 2009; Mazaheri & Jensen, 2010; Pomper & Ansorge, 2021; Womelsdorf et al., 2007; Xu et al., 2024).
text.formatted: By intentionally keeping competing rhythms out of phase, the control center ensures that task-irrelevant distractors arrive during the low-excitability trough of the cycle, effectively attenuating the interfering signals <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Bonnefond & Jensen, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b140">Helfrich et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b148">Huang et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b189">Mathewson et al., 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b190">Mazaheri & Jensen, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b247">Pomper & Ansorge, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b342">Womelsdorf et al., 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b346">Xu et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: In short, "learning" in CoCo-PaLM defines a process of changing how different representations communicate with one another.
This communication can be represented in longterm synaptic changes or short-term rhythmic gating.

In either case, the model's emphasis on the changes to the communication between representations contrasts with non-learning models, which instead attempt to explain interference in persistent activation of representations themselves.
Learning comes in different forms.
One important classification of learning mechanisms concerns the use of error signals.
Two prominent mechanisms in this regard include Hebbian learning (Hebb, 1949), which does not use error signals, and error-based learning (Rumelhart et al., 1986; Widrow & Hoff, 1960), which does.
text.formatted: Two prominent mechanisms in this regard include Hebbian learning <ref type="bibr" target="#b138">(Hebb, 1949)</ref>, which does not use error signals, and error-based learning <ref type="bibr">(Rumelhart et al., 1986;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b338">Widrow & Hoff, 1960)</ref>, which does.

text.text: Hebbian learning assumes that the co-activation of pre-and postsynaptic neurons correlates with the strengthening of their connection (Choe, 2022).
text.formatted: Hebbian learning assumes that the co-activation of pre-and postsynaptic neurons correlates with the strengthening of their connection <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">(Choe, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: This localized, activation-driven strengthening has been widely observed across multiple cortical and subcortical regions, most notably the hippocampus, further endorsing the use of Hebbian learning (Barrionuevo & Brown, 1983; Bliss & Gardner-Medwin, 1973; Bliss & Lømo, 1973; Dayan & Abbott, 2001; Dolphin et al., 1982; Frégnac, 2003; Gerstner & Kistler, 2002; McNaughton et al., 1978; Shouval, 2007).
text.formatted: This localized, activation-driven strengthening has been widely observed across multiple cortical and subcortical regions, most notably the hippocampus, further endorsing the use of Hebbian learning <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Barrionuevo & Brown, 1983;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Bliss & Gardner-Medwin, 1973;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Bliss & Lømo, 1973;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">Dayan & Abbott, 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b89">Dolphin et al., 1982;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b111">Frégnac, 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b122">Gerstner & Kistler, 2002;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b198">McNaughton et al., 1978;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b292">Shouval, 2007)</ref>.

text.text: Behaviorally, evidence for Hebbian learning comes from studies showing that errors are learned (e.g., language : Humphreys et al., 2010; McCandliss et al., 2002; Waller et al., 2024; memory: Marsh et al., 2007; McDermott, 1996; Roediger & Marsh, 2005; motor control: Diedrichsen et al., 2010; Huang et al., 2011).
text.formatted: Behaviorally, evidence for Hebbian learning comes from studies showing that errors are learned (e.g., language <ref type="bibr">: Humphreys et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b191">McCandliss et al., 2002;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b327">Waller et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr">memory: Marsh et al., 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b195">McDermott, 1996;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b261">Roediger & Marsh, 2005</ref>; motor control: <ref type="bibr" target="#b88">Diedrichsen et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b147">Huang et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Since nobody intends to learn or strengthen their own errors, and error-based learning mechanisms aim specifically to prevent errors from being repeated, learning one's errors is most compatible with Hebbian learning.

This learning mode is unsupervised and thus mirrors the ecological reality of many cognitive actions for which explicit feedback is not available in the environment or necessarily attended to (Linsker, 1986; McClelland, 2001; Rumelhart & Zipser, 1985; Waller et al., 2024; Whittington & Bogacz, 2019).
text.formatted: This learning mode is unsupervised and thus mirrors the ecological reality of many cognitive actions for which explicit feedback is not available in the environment or necessarily attended to <ref type="bibr" target="#b178">(Linsker, 1986;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b192">McClelland, 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b271">Rumelhart & Zipser, 1985;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b327">Waller et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b337">Whittington & Bogacz, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: However, Hebbian learning cannot be the whole story.
Humans can learn effectively from feedback when it is provided and attended to, and such feedback leads to faster and more efficient learning.

For example, attempting to answer a question and receiving correction after an error lead to better retention than studying the correct answer alone (Butterfield & Metcalfe, 2001; Chen et al., 2025; Kornell et al., 2009).
text.formatted: For example, attempting to answer a question and receiving correction after an error lead to better retention than studying the correct answer alone <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Butterfield & Metcalfe, 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">Chen et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b164">Kornell et al., 2009)</ref>.

text.text: In fact, many language studies have shown that allowing people to make mistakes and receive corrective feedback leads to better performance (Middleton et al., 2015; Saxton, 1997; Saxton et al., 1998; Schuchard & Middleton, 2018; cf. Fillingham et al., 2006; see Fillingham et al., 2003, and Middleton & Schwartz, 2012, for a review).

text.text: These findings form the basis for error-based learning (Rumelhart et al., 1986; Widrow & Hoff, 1960).
text.formatted: These findings form the basis for error-based learning <ref type="bibr">(Rumelhart et al., 1986;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b338">Widrow & Hoff, 1960)</ref>.

text.text: Error-based learning refers to adjustments that are driven by detecting a discrepancy between an anticipated and an actual outcome.
Since deviations can be directional (actual outcomes may be better or worse than expected outcomes), changes to connection weights can be directional as well.

Computationally, error-based learning in multi-layered networks had to be implemented through backpropagation, which has been criticized for potential lack of biological plausibility (Crick, 1989; Grossberg, 1987; Stork, 1989).
text.formatted: Computationally, error-based learning in multi-layered networks had to be implemented through backpropagation, which has been criticized for potential lack of biological plausibility <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">(Crick, 1989;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b130">Grossberg, 1987;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b305">Stork, 1989)</ref>.

text.text: However, more recent work has shown that error-based learning can be approximated in biologically plausible ways, for example, through local synaptic changes driven by differences in neural activity (Lillicrap et al., 2020; O'Reilly, 1996; Richards & Lillicrap, 2019; Sacramento et al., 2018; Whittington & Bogacz, 2019).
text.formatted: However, more recent work has shown that error-based learning can be approximated in biologically plausible ways, for example, through local synaptic changes driven by differences in neural activity <ref type="bibr" target="#b177">(Lillicrap et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b233">O'Reilly, 1996;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b256">Richards & Lillicrap, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b273">Sacramento et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b337">Whittington & Bogacz, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Both kinds of learning have been previously employed in models of interference in language production. Howard et al.'s (2006) model is a Hebbian learning model: It simply strengthens the connections between the selected word and its semantic features.
text.formatted: Both kinds of learning have been previously employed in models of interference in language production. <ref type="bibr">Howard et al.'s (2006)</ref> model is a Hebbian learning model: It simply strengthens the connections between the selected word and its semantic features.

text.text: In contrast, Oppenheim et al.'s (2010) model and its related models are error-based learning models.
text.formatted: In contrast, <ref type="bibr" target="#b231">Oppenheim et al.'s (2010)</ref> model and its related models are error-based learning models.

text.text: At the end of a trial, with targets and distractors activated, targets are assumed to be less activated than expected and distractors to be more activated than expected.
Subsequently, the weights between target words and semantic features are strengthened, and those between distractor words and semantic features are weakened.
Our choice of learning rules was driven by simplicity, allowing us to test where simpler mechanisms are sufficient and where, instead, more complex processing is required.
For contextual similarity, a simple Hebbian rule sufficed: No negative weight changes were necessary to produce the interference pattern in CN and BCN.
In contrast, capturing the correct sequential pattern of adaptive control in PWI required that weights be scaled by a conflict error signal.
Recall that on each trial, the running average of conflict was subtracted from the current conflict, thus determining whether the trial was harder or easier than expected.
A harder-than-expected trial provided a positive signal for weight updates, whereas an easier-than-expected trial provided a negative signal for weight updates.
This differential signal is critical for differential adjustments after congruent vs. incongruent trials, which are generally easier and harder than average, respectively.

In short, CoCo-PaLM takes advantage of both simple Hebbian learning (within modules) and error-based learning (between modules and the domain-general control center), with internal conflict acting as the external feedback (Verguts & Notebaert, 2008).
text.formatted: In short, CoCo-PaLM takes advantage of both simple Hebbian learning (within modules) and error-based learning (between modules and the domain-general control center), with internal conflict acting as the external feedback <ref type="bibr">(Verguts & Notebaert, 2008)</ref>.

text.text: One of the longest and most vigorous debates in language production research concerns how a word is selected among competing alternatives.
Two mechanisms are often considered: noncompetitive and competitive.
Non-competitive selection assumes an absolute selection threshold (Mahon et al., 2007; Navarrete et al., 2014).
text.formatted: Non-competitive selection assumes an absolute selection threshold <ref type="bibr" target="#b186">(Mahon et al., 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b209">Navarrete et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Any lexical item that passes that threshold can be selected, regardless of the activation of other lexical items.

Competitive selection (Abdel Rahman & Melinger, 2009; Roelofs, 2003 Roelofs, , 2018)), in contrast, assumes that a relative threshold is necessary for selection, with or without an absolute threshold.
text.formatted: Competitive selection <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Abdel Rahman & Melinger, 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b264">Roelofs, 2003</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b265">Roelofs, , 2018))</ref>, in contrast, assumes that a relative threshold is necessary for selection, with or without an absolute threshold.

text.text: In other words, competitive selection assumes that a lexical item must be more activated than its competitors by at least a certain amount before selection can proceed.

Originally, the debate centered around facilitatory vs. inhibitory influence of semantically related items; proponents of non-competitive selection often appealed to the facilitatory effect of thematic relations (e.g., Alario et al., 2000; Costa et al., 2005; McDonagh et al., 2020; Mirman et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2023), whereas proponents of competitive selection cited the interference induced by taxonomic cohorts (e.g., Schriefers et al., 1990).
text.formatted: Originally, the debate centered around facilitatory vs. inhibitory influence of semantically related items; proponents of non-competitive selection often appealed to the facilitatory effect of thematic relations (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Alario et al., 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">Costa et al., 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b196">McDonagh et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b206">Mirman et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b351">Zhang et al., 2023)</ref>, whereas proponents of competitive selection cited the interference induced by taxonomic cohorts (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b281">Schriefers et al., 1990)</ref>.

text.text: However, recent modeling work has shown that the dual effect of semantically similar items can be explained without assuming one selection mechanism or another (Oppenheim & Nozari, 2024).
text.formatted: However, recent modeling work has shown that the dual effect of semantically similar items can be explained without assuming one selection mechanism or another <ref type="bibr" target="#b232">(Oppenheim & Nozari, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Both mechanisms can produce facilitation or interference depending on the configuration of the semantic space and the timeline of activation of semantic features, which are more relevant to the differences between thematic and taxonomic similarity than selection rules, per se.
The question thus remains, which selection rule is the correct one?
Here, we have opted for a competitive selection rule (Howard et al., 2006; Roelofs, 2003 Roelofs, , 2018)).
text.formatted: Here, we have opted for a competitive selection rule <ref type="bibr" target="#b145">(Howard et al., 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b264">Roelofs, 2003</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b265">Roelofs, , 2018))</ref>.

text.text: However, we do not view the selection process as an either-or choice.
Rather, we believe that a flexible criterion provides the best account of selection in a system such as language production, which can easily adapt to new goals (Nozari & Hepner, 2019a , 2019b).
text.formatted: Rather, we believe that a flexible criterion provides the best account of selection in a system such as language production, which can easily adapt to new goals <ref type="bibr" target="#b221">(Nozari & Hepner, 2019a</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b222">, 2019b)</ref>.

text.text: Specifically, if accuracy is an important goal (choosing between "probability" and "likelihood" while teaching statistics to a class), speakers would want to ensure that they have the correct word before producing it.
This can be achieved by setting a high relative threshold (a conservative criterion).

Conversely, when accuracy is not an important goal (choosing between "probability" and "likelihood" when talking about the chance of rain to a friend), and multiple alternatives achieve the same communicative goal, speakers may choose to opt for a low relative threshold (a liberal criterion).
If the relative threshold is low enough, selection effectively becomes non-competitive.
Put differently, an inherently competitive selection mechanism can easily become noncompetitive based on task goals, if it has a flexible criterion.
In contrast, a purely non-competitive selection mechanism cannot simply become competitive on demand.

Furthermore, there is abundant evidence that the brain can keep track of competing alternatives (here and elsewhere formalized as conflict; e.g., Botvinick et al., 2001; Nozari et al., 2011), which would be futile in a purely non-competitive system.
text.formatted: Furthermore, there is abundant evidence that the brain can keep track of competing alternatives (here and elsewhere formalized as conflict; e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Botvinick et al., 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b218">Nozari et al., 2011)</ref>, which would be futile in a purely non-competitive system.

text.text: For these reasons, we adopted a competitive selection rule.
All current simulations target tasks in which accuracy is emphasized.
To capture this, we chose a threshold not close to zero.
However, this parameter can be easily changed to capture situations in which accuracy is not emphasized.
The term inhibitory control has been used widely and loosely in the language production literature.
As explained in the Introduction, evidence of behavioral interference has often been taken to imply the involvement of inhibitory control.
Moreover, the term is often taken to represent a unitary mechanism.

One of the main claims of the current study, supported by behavioral and neural data, and borne out by the simulations, is that there is more than one mechanism for the generation of interference and resolution of the ensuing conflict (see also Quinn et al., 2025).
text.formatted: One of the main claims of the current study, supported by behavioral and neural data, and borne out by the simulations, is that there is more than one mechanism for the generation of interference and resolution of the ensuing conflict (see also <ref type="bibr" target="#b250">Quinn et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Specifically, when stimulus-driven information is generally sufficient to guide processing towards the correct response, as in the case of interference induced by contextual similarity, languageinternal processes suffice.
In contrast, when stimulus-driven information generally leads to the wrong response, as when prepotent distractors are present, language-external mechanisms are needed.

Interference induced by contextual similarity has been captured by two mechanisms in previous computational models: either competitive selection (e.g., current study; as well as competitive selection mechanism.

Biologically, competitive selection can be captured by lateral inhibition (Kohonen, 1982; Linsker, 1986; Rumelhart & Zipser, 1985) or mutual inhibitory connections between competing representations for which there is an abundance of evidence (Adesnik & Naka, 2018; Douglas & Martin, 2004; Fishell & Kepecs, 2020; Hartline & Ratliff, 1957; Isaacson & Scanziani, 2011; Snyder et al., 2010).
text.formatted: Biologically, competitive selection can be captured by lateral inhibition <ref type="bibr" target="#b162">(Kohonen, 1982;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b178">Linsker, 1986;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b271">Rumelhart & Zipser, 1985)</ref> or mutual inhibitory connections between competing representations for which there is an abundance of evidence <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Adesnik & Naka, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b90">Douglas & Martin, 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b108">Fishell & Kepecs, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b136">Hartline & Ratliff, 1957;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b154">Isaacson & Scanziani, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b297">Snyder et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: The ubiquity of lateral inhibition across various sensory-motor domains shows its domain-generality as a computational principle.
However, the implementation is clearly local, sharing no neural machinery across domains.
In case of contextual similarity, these local processes are sufficient to resolve conflict.
In contrast, a prepotent distractor induces interference by virtue of having a priori stronger S-R mapping than the target.
As such, lateral inhibition between the target and the distractor will generally be resolved in favor of the distractor, leading to the wrong response.
This necessitates the involvement of a goal-directed process that can override the prepotent S-R mapping.
In CoCo-PaLM, this top-down process is modeled as a language-external monitoring-control loop.
Goal maintenance is implemented through the adjustment of the connection between set goals in the control center and the relevant and irrelevant task dimensions.
Recall that, in the context of the weights between the control center and dimensions, weight adjustments are a proxy for short-term reorientation.

Two factors determine the direction and magnitude of these weight changes: the conflict error signal and parameter B. As explained earlier, harder-and easier-than-expected trials generate positive and negative conflict error signals, respectively, prompting positive and negative weight changes.

However, this signal is also modulated by B. The thorough parameter space exploration of B showed that for the correct CSE pattern to be obtained, B must be set to induce strong negative adjustments to the weights connected with irrelevant information.
This analysis clearly points to the critical role of central inhibition in tasks with a prepotent distractor.
In short, the results suggest that lexical retrieval in the absence of a prepotent distractor, at best requires local (lateral) inhibition.
In contrast, central inhibition is required when a prepotent distractor is present.
This is not to say that central inhibition cannot possibly be involved in the former case.
Any task can benefit from greater focus on goal-relevant information (Nozari, 2025b; Nozari, Mirman, & Thompson-Schill, 2016).
text.formatted: Any task can benefit from greater focus on goal-relevant information <ref type="bibr" target="#b217">(Nozari, 2025b;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b225">Nozari, Mirman, & Thompson-Schill, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Rather, the key claim is that the involvement of central inhibition in such cases is optional, rather than critical.

In line with this optionality, regions often associated with the central monitoring-control loop have sometimes been identified in resolving contextual similarity (Abel et al., 2009 (Abel et al., , 2012;; de Zubicaray & McMahon, 2009; de Zubicaray et al., 2013) but not always (Gauvin et al., 2021; Rizio et al., 2017; Spalek & Thompson-Schill, 2008).

text.text: While providing a detailed neurobiological model is clearly beyond the scope of this paper, we present a brief neural mapping of the model in this section for two reasons.
The first reason is to show that the model has the potential to be fully neurally mapped in the future.
The second reason is that linking model components and parameters to neural regions can help with understanding their function.

The core language model in CoCo-PaLM includes a largely distributed semantic network, aligned with modern theories of semantic processing (see Binder & Desai, 2011; Lambon Ralph et al., 2017; Pulvermüller, 2013, for reviews).

text.text: The domain-general monitoring-control loop in CoCo-PaLM is modeled after the frontoparietal network, especially the prefrontal cortex (PFC), as conceived of by Miller and Cohen (2001).
text.formatted: The domain-general monitoring-control loop in CoCo-PaLM is modeled after the frontoparietal network, especially the prefrontal cortex (PFC), as conceived of by <ref type="bibr" target="#b204">Miller and Cohen (2001)</ref>.

text.text: These authors proposed that cognitive control arises from the PFC's capacity to actively maintain patterns of neural activity representing goals and the rules needed to achieve them.

These prefrontal representations function as a modulatory network, sending excitatory top-down bias signals to widespread downstream structures, guiding the flow of neural activity along the specific neural pathways needed in the task.
PFC implements task goals and moderates performance through two distinct albeit interactive functions (Nozari, 2025b): monitoring and control.
text.formatted: PFC implements task goals and moderates performance through two distinct albeit interactive functions <ref type="bibr" target="#b217">(Nozari, 2025b)</ref>: monitoring and control.

text.text: The medial prefrontal cortex, especially the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) acts as the monitor, combining interoceptive effort costs and goal values (Botvinick et al., 2001; Brown & Braver, 2005; Kok, 2022; Shenhav et al., 2013; Verguts et al., 2015).
text.formatted: The medial prefrontal cortex, especially the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) acts as the monitor, combining interoceptive effort costs and goal values <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Botvinick et al., 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Brown & Braver, 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b163">Kok, 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b289">Shenhav et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b323">Verguts et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: As such, ACC is consistently involved in conflict-inducing paradigms, such as the Stroop and Simon tasks (Barch et al., 2001; Hanslmayr et al., 2008; Milham et al., 2001; Piai et al., 2013; Swick & Jovanovic, 2002).

text.text: The question remains: how does PFC select representations?
Much evidence points to subcortical structures, especially the basal ganglia, for this role.

Studies have shown that basal ganglia receive converging projections from large parts of the cortex, but relay only selective information to PFC via thalamus (Albin et al., 1989; Alexander et al., 1986; DeLong, 1990; Gurney et al., 2001; Kemp & Powell, 1971; Redgrave et al., 1999; Stephenson-Jones et al., 2011).

text.text: Importantly, such selection is not confined to motor programs, and encompass cognitive information as well (Frank et al., 2007; Houk et al., 2007; Humphries et al., 2006; O'Reilly & Frank, 2006; Stewart et al., 2010; Stocco & Lebiere, 2014; Stocco et al., 2010).

text.text: It is widely agreed that the information selection process results from the competition between two main pathways, direct and indirect, which have excitatory and inhibitory effects on thalamus, respectively (Albin et al., 1989; DeLong, 1990).

text.text: To optimize performance, the two pathways must reach a balance for relaying the most relevant information and keeping out the irrelevant information (O' Reilly & Frank, 2006; Stocco et al., 2010).

text.text: In CoCo-PaLM, parameter B most closely captures the role of the basal ganglia.

The positive and negative weight changes to the relevant and irrelevant information, respectively, represent the balance between the direct and indirect pathways, biasing competition towards the relevant information.
Recall that the parameter space search showed that adjustments were mainly driven by negative adjustments to the irrelevant weights, suggesting a more prominent role for the indirect pathway.

Incidentally, in cognitive tasks with interfering distractors, the indirect pathway has been shown to play a particularly prominent role by discarding irrelevant information (e.g., McNab & Klingberg, 2008; Stocco et al., 2017).

text.text: Results of Simulation 5 showed that even assuming full neural domain-generality of the control center does not necessarily lead to functional domain-generality of control.

CoCo-PaLM is well-positioned to test this issue, since we intentionally used a single pair of task nodes in the control center, unlike previous control models that have used different task nodes for different tasks (e.g., Verguts & Notebaert, 2008).

text.text: Nevertheless, we showed that implementing control in the connections between a domain-general control center and domain-specific representations still leads to functional domain-specificity of control, simply because training one set of control weights does not change other control weights.

This finding is well-aligned with the absence of notable positive cross-task CSEs (Akçay & Hazeltine, 2011; Egner et al., 2007; Freund & Nozari, 2018; Funes et al., 2010; Notebaert & Verguts, 2008; Wendt et al., 2006; Zhang et al., 2025; Zhu, Wang, et al., 2025) and the absence of far transfer in training studies (Melby-Lervåg & Hulme, 2013; Owen et al., 2010; Redick et al., 2013; Sala et al., 2019; Sala & Gobet, 2019; Shipstead et al., 2012; Simons et al., 2016; Thompson et al., 2013).

text.text: The dissociation between the neural domain-generality of control and its functional domain-specificity also questions the logic of using analysis of individual differences as a reliable method for determining whether a task requires central inhibition or not.

Here, we refer to correlational studies, where the size of interference in task A is correlated with the size of interference in a task such as Stroop, flanker, or Simon (or a combination of them), to determine whether task A requires domain-general inhibitory control or not (e.g., Brown-Schmidt, 2009; Nozari & Omaki, 2018; Nozari, Trueswell, & Thompson-Schill, 2016; Shao et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Here, we refer to correlational studies, where the size of interference in task A is correlated with the size of interference in a task such as Stroop, flanker, or Simon (or a combination of them), to determine whether task A requires domain-general inhibitory control or not (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Brown-Schmidt, 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b227">Nozari & Omaki, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b229">Nozari, Trueswell, & Thompson-Schill, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b287">Shao et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: To understand the problem with this argument, let us use a simple example: you and your neighbor both receive electricity from the same power plant (a proxy for domain-general control regions in the brain).
Does the shared power plant predict a correlation between the electrical status of your respective houses?
Yes and no.
If something goes wrong in the power plant, you both lose electricity, so the weakening or removal of the shared resource affects both of you negatively.

This is the correlation often observed in patients with damage to domain-general control regions (e.g., PFC), who show impairment across a wide variety of tasks that tap control (Alvarez & Emory, 2006; Barbey et al., 2012; Burgess & Shallice, 1996; Gläscher et al., 2012; Jones & Graff-Radford, 2021; Nozari, 2019; Stuss & Alexander, 2000; Woolgar et al., 2010 Woolgar et al., , 2018)).
text.formatted: This is the correlation often observed in patients with damage to domain-general control regions (e.g., PFC), who show impairment across a wide variety of tasks that tap control <ref type="bibr">(Alvarez & Emory, 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Barbey et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">Burgess & Shallice, 1996;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b123">Gläscher et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b156">Jones & Graff-Radford, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b214">Nozari, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b308">Stuss & Alexander, 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b345">Woolgar et al., 2010</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b343">Woolgar et al., , 2018))</ref>.

text.text: But what if the power plant is up and running at full capacity?
Can you predict the electrical capabilities of your neighbor based on what you can do in your own house?
The answer is no.

For example, you may be able to install an electric vehicle charger in your house, but your neighbor may not, because the capacity depends not only on the shared power plant but also on the cables between the power plant and your individual houses, as well as the type of fuse box and other appliances consuming electricity in each house.
Therefore, despite having the shared power plant, you cannot know with certainty the electrical capabilities of your neighbor based on your own.
By extension, in a neurotypical system, a shared neural resource is not by itself sufficient to predict function across two different domains.
A similar logic holds for training.

If control is implemented in the connections between domain-general control center and domain-specific task dimensions, achieving results is contingent on training those weights within the context of the task, or a task similar enough to train the relevant dimension.
But what about cases where a positive correlation is observed?
We believe that such cases may reflect a common parameter in the control implementation across tasks.

For example, in our model, we kept B, which is responsible for biasing competition away from the irrelevant and towards the relevant information, the same across PWI and PP, to keep free parameters to a minimum.
However, B may very well differ across tasks.
Similarly, the conflict error signal can, and often does, depend on task difficulty and can differ from task to task.
Therefore, while a positive correlation in the size of interference may signal some common parameters, a null effect does not refute relying on central monitoring-control loops.
For this reason, correlational analysis of individual differences is an unreliable tool for examining the role of inhibitory control in a given task or operation.

Rather, simple heuristics, such as the insufficiency of stimulus-driven information for guiding the process towards the correct response, can be much more informative in determining whether a task does or does not require central control.

In brief, we demonstrate that computationally implementing cognitive control and how it interacts with various tasks, provides a path forward for cognitive transfer studies: Computational implementation allows to predict what exactly transfers between which tasks, and how such transfer should be measured.
CoCo-PaLM was able to capture the dynamics of interference induced by both contextual similarity and the presence of a prepotent response.

Two key elements in the model account for its explanatory power: its hierarchical architecture (with modules embedded in the domain-general monitoring-control loop) and its use of learning at each level to explain how interference arises and is mitigated.
Hebbian learning within the domain-specific task modules appears sufficient for explaining the data on contextual similarity.

In contrast, learning in the domain-general monitoring control center is necessary for explaining the data on prepotent response distraction and interactions between language and non-linguistic tasks.
We further showed that this framework can explain the dynamics of control transfer between tasks.

Specifically, even assuming full neural domain-generality of control is insufficient to expect functional transfer of control between tasks, at least when they do not share relevant or irrelevant dimensions.
With this foundation in place, future work can focus on how overlap in task-relevant or irrelevant dimensions can modulate such transfer.

Therefore, by exploring the space of parameters that give us the correct CSE, we can examine whether obtaining the correct CSE pattern depends critically on the inhibition of irrelevant information, or it can also be obtained simply with stronger positive changes to the relevant weights.
To this end, we conducted 1,000 simulations for each combination of 𝐴𝐴 𝑐𝑐.𝑅𝑅 -𝐵𝐵 and 𝐴𝐴 𝑐𝑐.𝐼𝐼𝑅𝑅 -𝐵𝐵.
For the former, a range of 0-1 was considered, since negative changes to weights that carry relevant information are conceptually meaningless.
For the latter, a wider range of -2.5 to 2.5 (step size = 0.5) was considered, to investigate the importance of inhibition through negative values.

text.text: The pattern is clear: the only combination that produces the correct CSE is a pairing of positive 𝐴𝐴 𝑐𝑐.𝑅𝑅 -𝐵𝐵 and negative 𝐴𝐴 𝑐𝑐.𝐼𝐼𝑅𝑅 -𝐵𝐵.
In other words, inhibiting the weights that support the processing of irrelevant information is critical to obtaining the correct CSE pattern in PWI.

The combination of the conflict error signal and a B that biases competition away from the irrelevant information produces the full CSE pattern: when the conflict signal is positive (generally after an incongruent trial), relevant weights grow stronger and irrelevant weights grow weaker.
The exaggerated difference between the two sets of weights focuses the model on the relevant information and makes the following incongruent trial easier.
Conversely, when the conflict signal is negative (generally after a congruent trial), relevant weights grow smaller and irrelevant weights slightly larger.
This diminished difference between the two sets of weights allows the model to use both sources of input and makes the next congruent trial easier.
One might ask, why would the model ever decrease the difference between relevant and irrelevant weights?
Note that the model this question constitutes Step 1 in our approach.

Once we determine if one or more mechanisms underlie conflict resolution in lexical retrieval, Step 2 involves determining the key characteristics of tasks and findings that fall under each mechanism.

Understanding these characteristics serves two purposes: (a) they constrain the computations relevant to the mechanism(s), and (b) they highlight potential similarities and differences in control mechanisms.

Step 3 formalizes these characteristics into computational principles, evaluates current computational models of language production in light of those principles, and formulates the criteria for an improved model.
Finally, Step 4 implements this model and tests it on empirical data.

In what follows, we first describe the core lexical model in detail.

We then present two sets of simulations for contextual similarity-Simulation 1 for CN and Simulation 2 for BCNshowing that the core model can by itself explain the empirical data from both of these tasks, without the need for any parameter changes.
Next, Simulation 3 demonstrates that the core model alone is insufficient for modeling the PWI data, necessitating the involvement of the monitoringcontrol loop.
Simulation 4 then uses CoCo-PaLM to model CSE in PWI.
Finally, Simulation 5 embeds a second, visuospatial task PP in the domain-general monitoring-control loop, and models cross-task CSE between PWI and this new task.
